AZ-01.title: Arizona District 1 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: AZ-1 — Scottsdale, Paradise Valley, Fountain Hills, Cave Creek and north Phoenix; an affluent, highly educated suburban seat where independents (35%) nearly match Republicans (38%). Open seat; Cook, Inside Elections and Sabato all rate it a Toss Up.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Rep. David Schweikert (R), in Congress since 2011, gave up the seat to run for governor but lost the July 21 Republican primary to Andy Biggs (74.0% to about 14%).
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Feely 49.8%, Chaplik 35.7%, Trobough 14.5%; Democrats — Shah 39.4%, Galán-Woods 34.4%, Treble 17.7%, McCartney 8.5% in the July 21 primary. November ballot: Jay Feely (R), Amish Shah (D) and Monica Alponte (Libertarian, unopposed in the July 21 Libertarian primary); any other third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October; write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Jay Feely (R), a former NFL kicker for the Arizona Cardinals and CBS Sports analyst, faces Dr. Amish Shah (D), a Mayo Clinic emergency physician and former state representative who beat the national party's preferred candidate in the primary.
  • Voting History: Schweikert held the seat narrowly in both recent cycles — 51.9% to 48.1% over Shah in 2024 (+3.8) and 50.4% to 49.6% over Jevin Hodge in 2022 (+0.8).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Cost of living, housing and water supply dominate a fast-growing desert suburb; abortion access remains a mobilising issue for Democrats, and data-centre expansion in the Valley is drawing scrutiny.
  • National Alignment: Feely runs on extending Trump's tax cuts, deregulation and domestic manufacturing; Shah blames tariffs for higher grocery, fuel, car and housing costs and campaigns on healthcare and housing affordability.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Toss Up (Sept 25); Inside Elections Toss-up (Oct 1); Sabato Toss-up (Sept 29). Public polls: GBAO, a Democratic polling firm (Aug 21–24, 500 likely voters), Feely 46%, Shah 44%; Peak Insights, a Republican polling firm (Aug 17–20, 400 likely voters), Feely 53%, Shah 42%; GBAO (June 11–15), Feely 44%, Shah 41%, Alponte 7%. Through the July 1 pre-primary reporting date, Feely had raised $2.5M to Shah's $1.8M.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Shah, the son of Gujarati immigrants, would join the Indian-American caucus in Congress if elected; no India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

sections.html:

  • Arizona Mirror (azmirror.com) — Nonprofit newsroom covering state politics and campaigns
  • KJZZ (kjzz.org) — Phoenix public radio; Valley politics and water reporting
  • KTAR News (ktar.com) — Phoenix news radio; candidate profiles and issue comparisons
  • Noble Predictive Insights (noblepredictive.com) — Phoenix pollster; regular Arizona statewide surveys

CA-04.title: California District 4 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Proposition 50 redrew this seat with nearly 50% new territory: it now runs from Napa and Sonoma wine country east across the Sacramento Valley into Sacramento, Yolo, Sutter, Yuba, Lake, Colusa and Placer counties, taking in more rural, conservative voters (CapRadio). It remains comfortably Democratic — and the general election is a Democrat-versus-Democrat contest.
  • Incumbent Status: Mike Thompson (D), in the House since 1999 and a senior member of the Ways and Means Committee; running for a 15th term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): June 2 top-two primary (official Statement of Vote): Mike Thompson (D) 41.0%, Eric Jones (D) 22.2%, Ray Riehle (R) 20.7%; five other Republicans shared a further 15.4%. November ballot (top-two system, per the certified June 2 Statement of Vote): Mike Thompson (D) and Eric Jones (D); write-in candidates not listed. Riehle has since endorsed Jones and pledged to help build Republican support for him (CalMatters).

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Mike Thompson (D), 75, a Vietnam veteran and 27-year incumbent backed by Newsom, Padilla and Schiff, faces Eric Jones (D), 35, a self-funding former venture capitalist running on generational change and courting Republican and centrist voters.
  • Voting History: Thompson won 66.5% to 33.5% over John Munn (R) in 2024 (+33.0) and 67.8% to 32.2% over Matt Brock (R) in 2022 (+35.6), both under the pre-2026 lines.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Wildfire resilience and insurance, agricultural disaster aid and water infrastructure (including the Sites Reservoir) dominate; Thompson argues his seniority secures federal money for these. Jones attacks Thompson's donations from pharmaceutical, insurance and PG&E interests as "corporate cronyism" (CalMatters).
  • National Alignment: Thompson prioritises ending the Iran conflict and backs ICE reforms such as warrants and body cameras. Jones champions Medicare for All, an income-tax exemption for earners under $150,000 and congressional term limits, and attacks war spending as crowding out healthcare (CapRadio).

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid D (as of Sept 25); not on Inside Elections' (Oct 1) or Sabato's (Sept 29) competitive lists (i.e. safe). Both November candidates are Democrats. No independent public poll was found as of 3 October. FEC filings through June 30: Thompson had raised $4.20M with $1.08M cash on hand; Jones had raised $8.38M, including about $5.4M of his own money, with $656,000 on hand (FEC).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026. Thompson's seat on Ways and Means gives him a role on trade legislation, including tariffs affecting US–India trade.

CA-11.title: California District 11 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: California's 11th covers most of San Francisco and remains one of the most Democratic seats in the country; it was not a Proposition 50 target and stays overwhelmingly Democratic (Harris won roughly 82% to 14% under the pre-2026 lines). The contest is a Democrat-versus-Democrat general election under the top-two system.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Nancy Pelosi (D), who has held the seat since 1987 and served twice as Speaker, is retiring at the end of her term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Eleven candidates (eight Democrats, two Republicans, one independent) ran in the June 2 top-two primary. Certified count: Scott Wiener (D) 40.7%, Connie Chan (D) 29.7%, Saikat Chakrabarti (D) 17.9%. Wiener and Chan advanced. November ballot (top-two system, per the certified June 2 Statement of Vote): Scott Wiener (D) and Connie Chan (D); write-in candidates not listed. Pelosi endorsed Chan on 18 May and Chakrabarti later converted his campaign committee into a PAC backing Chan (Mission Local).

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: State Senator Scott Wiener (D), a pro-housing legislator and author of California's 2025 AI-safety law, faces Supervisor Connie Chan (D), a labour-backed progressive endorsed by Pelosi and Senator Adam Schiff.
  • Voting History: Pelosi won 81.0% to 19.0% over Bruce Lou (R) in 2024 (+62.0) and 84.0% to 16.0% over John Dennis (R) in 2022 (+68.0).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Housing supply is the central dividing line: Wiener built his career on upzoning laws, while Chan is attacked for approving fewer new homes than any other supervisor since 2021 (CalMatters, 2 Oct). AI regulation and labour are the second axis — Chan, backed by the California Labor Federation and SEIU, calls for a data-centre moratorium and union input on AI oversight; Wiener points to his state AI-safety statute.
  • National Alignment: Both are anti-Trump progressives who oppose Trump's proposed $1.5 trillion defence budget and oppose strikes on Iran without congressional authorisation; both describe Israel's conduct in Gaza as genocide, though Wiener still backs funding defensive systems such as Iron Dome while Chan opposes all arms sales (Mission Local). Both support universal health coverage and oppose sending US troops if China attacks Taiwan.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid D (as of Sept 25); not on Inside Elections' (Oct 1) or Sabato's (Sept 29) competitive lists (i.e. safe). Both November candidates are Democrats. No independent poll was found as of 3 October; a Chan campaign internal (Lake Research, July 14–19) had Wiener 45%, Chan 40%, and a PPP poll for a housing ballot committee (June 26–27) had Wiener 39%, Chan 38% (Mission Local). For May 14–June 30, Wiener raised $571,000 and held over $1.2M cash on hand; Chan raised $441,000 with $362,000 on hand.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026. Tech-policy relevance: Wiener authored California's 2025 AI-safety law and the seat covers San Francisco's AI industry, where H-1B and AI-governance questions affect Indian tech workers and firms.

sections.html:

CA-13.title: California District 13 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Northern San Joaquin Valley agricultural seat spanning Merced and parts of Stanislaus, San Joaquin, Madera and Fresno counties, with a large Latino electorate. Proposition 50 added south Stockton, moving the seat from Trump +5 to roughly Harris +1 on 2024 presidential results (Inside Elections).
  • Incumbent Status: Adam Gray (D), first elected in 2024 after a decade in the State Assembly; running for a second term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): June 2 top-two primary (official Statement of Vote): Adam Gray (D) 42.0%, Kevin Lincoln (R) 27.7%, Vin Kruttiventi (R) 15.2%, Daniel Garibay Rodriguez (D) 15.1%. Gray and Lincoln advanced. November ballot (top-two system, per the certified June 2 Statement of Vote): Adam Gray (D) and Kevin Lincoln (R); write-in candidates not listed. Lincoln, endorsed by Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, switched to this seat from CA-9 after Prop 50 passed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Adam Gray (D), a centrist who stresses bipartisanship, faces Kevin Lincoln II (R), a Marine veteran and pastor who was Stockton mayor from 2021 to 2024 and lost a 2024 bid in CA-9.
  • Voting History: Gray unseated John Duarte (R) 50.0% to 50.0% in 2024, a 187-vote margin and the last House race called that cycle; Duarte had won the 2022 race 50.2% to 49.8% (+0.4). Both results were under the pre-2026 lines.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Water deliveries for farmers and new storage are the dominant issue — Gray calls water the "number one issue" constituents raise (CBS Sacramento). Healthcare and food aid matter heavily: more than half of residents rely on Medi-Cal or ACA marketplace cover and about 48,000 households on SNAP. Lincoln campaigns on cost of living and "keeping the woke DEI agenda out of the Valley".
  • National Alignment: Gray emphasises independence from his party — he was the only California Democrat to vote to end the autumn 2025 government shutdown, citing SNAP and healthcare (Gray office, Nov 2025). Lincoln runs as a Trump-endorsed Republican, attacking Washington Democrats over grocery, fuel and housing costs.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Lean D (as of Sept 25); Inside Elections Tilt D (as of Oct 1); Sabato Leans D (as of Sept 29). No independent public poll was found as of 3 October. FEC filings through June 30: Gray had raised $4.19M with $2.07M cash on hand; Lincoln had raised $2.24M (including $788,000 in transfers) with $838,000 on hand (FEC).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Vin Kruttiventi, a Pleasanton-based first-generation immigrant from India and consulting-firm CEO, finished third in the Republican field (15.2%) and is out of the race (campaign site). No India-specific position by either general-election candidate was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

sections.html:

  • Stocktonia (stocktonia.org) — Nonprofit Stockton newsroom; covers Lincoln's record as mayor
  • KVPR Valley Public Radio (kvpr.org) — Central Valley public radio

  • PPIC Statewide Survey (ppic.org) — Nonpartisan statewide surveys

CA-22.title: California District 22 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Southern San Joaquin Valley seat across Kern, Kings and Tulare counties, majority-Latino and heavily agricultural; Proposition 50 added east Bakersfield and other Democratic-leaning areas. Under the new lines Trump would have carried it by about 2 points in 2024 (50% to 48%), versus roughly 6 points under the old map (Inside Elections).
  • Incumbent Status: David Valadao (R), in Congress 2013–19 and again since 2021; running for re-election.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): June 2 top-two primary (official Statement of Vote): David G. Valadao (R) 40.7%, Randy Villegas (D) 32.4%, Jasmeet Bains (D) 26.9%. November ballot (top-two system, per the certified June 2 Statement of Vote): David Valadao (R) and Randy Villegas (D); write-in candidates not listed. Villegas, backed by Bernie Sanders, beat Assemblymember Bains, the establishment favourite; a Republican-funded super PAC spent to boost Villegas as the weaker opponent (GV Wire).

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: David Valadao (R), a Hanford dairy farmer and one of ten House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump in 2021, faces Randy Villegas (D), a Visalia school-board trustee and college political scientist running as a Medicare for All populist.
  • Voting History: Valadao beat Rudy Salas (D) 53.4% to 46.6% in 2024 (+6.8) and 51.5% to 48.5% in 2022 (+3.0), both under the pre-2026 lines.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Medi-Cal is the dominant issue: about 64% of residents of Valadao's district rely on it, the highest share of any Republican-held seat, and Valadao voted for Trump's 2025 megabill cutting over $1 trillion from Medicaid (KVPR). Water supply for agriculture and the drift of Latino voters back towards Democrats after 2024 are the other key dynamics.
  • National Alignment: Valadao defends the Medicaid vote as protecting core recipients and avoiding tax rises, while campaigning on water, inflation and jobs. Villegas runs a left-populist campaign on wages, housing and Medicare for All, tying Valadao to Trump's healthcare cuts.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings diverge: Cook Toss Up (as of Sept 25); Inside Elections Toss-up (as of Oct 1); Sabato Leans D (as of Sept 29), after Democrats won 59% of the two-party primary vote (Porterville Recorder). No independent public poll was found as of 3 October. FEC filings through June 30: Valadao had raised $4.93M with $3.37M cash on hand; Villegas had raised $2.65M with $572,000 on hand (FEC).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Jasmeet Bains, a Bakersfield physician and the first Indian-origin Sikh woman elected to the California Assembly, was eliminated in the primary (The Tribune). No India-specific position by either general-election candidate was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

sections.html:

  • KVPR Valley Public Radio (kvpr.org) — Central Valley public radio; detailed Medi-Cal coverage
  • GV Wire (gvwire.com) — Fresno-based digital news; Valley politics
  • CalMatters (calmatters.org) — Nonprofit statewide newsroom

CA-40.title: California District 40 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Proposition 50 packed Republican voters into this newly redrawn district, which runs from eastern Orange County (Villa Park, Mission Viejo) through Corona and the Inland Empire to Murrieta and Menifee in Riverside County. Trump would have carried it by about 12 points in 2024 (Inside Elections); it contains 51% of Ken Calvert's old constituents, 33% of Young Kim's and 15% of Darrell Issa's.
  • Incumbent Status: Two Republican incumbents are running against each other: Ken Calvert (R), in the House since 1993 (previously CA-41) and Young Kim (R), elected in 2020 (currently CA-40).
  • Top Contenders (primary results): June 2 top-two primary (official Statement of Vote): Ken Calvert (R) 34.9%, Young Kim (R) 20.6%, Esther Kim-Varet (D) 16.6%, Lisa Ramirez (D) 14.0%, Joe Kerr (D) 8.6%. Democrats split their vote across five candidates and were locked out of the general election. November ballot (top-two system, per the certified June 2 Statement of Vote): Ken Calvert (R) and Young Kim (R); write-in candidates not listed. Trump did not endorse in the primary (NY1).

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: A Republican member-versus-member contest: Ken Calvert (R), a 33-year veteran who chairs the House Appropriations defence subcommittee, faces Young Kim (R), a three-term member and one of the first Korean American women in Congress, who chairs the Foreign Affairs East Asia and Pacific subcommittee.
  • Voting History: Redrawn district. Kim won the old CA-40 55.3% to 44.7% over Joe Kerr (D) in 2024 (+10.6) and 56.8% to 43.2% over Asif Mahmood (D) in 2022 (+13.6). Calvert won the old CA-41 51.7% to 48.3% over Will Rollins (D) in 2024 (+3.4) and 52.3% to 47.6% in 2022 (+4.7).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Home turf is the central argument: Calvert stresses his Corona roots and the infrastructure and defence money he has steered to Southern California, while Kim says "this is my district" and stresses bipartisan effectiveness and term limits (NY1). With no Democrat on the ballot, the 43% of primary voters who backed Democratic candidates could decide the outcome.
  • National Alignment: Both backed Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill" and tougher border policy, but they compete over Trump loyalty: Calvert brands Kim a "Trump-hating politician" from the party's moderate wing, noting she voted to certify Biden's 2020 win while he did not; Kim's ads attacked Calvert for having "begged Trump like a dog" for an endorsement (CBS LA).

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid R (as of Sept 25); not on Inside Elections' (Oct 1) or Sabato's (Sept 29) competitive lists (i.e. safe). Both November candidates are Republicans. No public general-election poll was found as of 3 October. FEC filings through June 30: Calvert had raised $6.14M with $1.50M cash on hand; Kim had raised $8.84M with $1.68M on hand (FEC).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Both candidates carry India-relevant portfolios. Kim, as chair of the Foreign Affairs East Asia and Pacific subcommittee, co-led with Gregory Meeks the Strengthening the Quad Act (reintroduced February 2025), which mandates a State Department Quad strategy with India, Japan and Australia and a Quad inter-parliamentary working group (Kim press release). Calvert chairs the Appropriations defence subcommittee, which funds US defence programmes including cooperation with partners.

CA-41.title: California District 41 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Proposition 50 turned the 41st from Ken Calvert's Republican Riverside County seat into a Democratic district in the southeast Los Angeles County suburbs — Downey, Whittier and neighbouring Gateway Cities — with a sliver of Orange County. Harris won about 56% there in 2024 under the new lines (Inside Elections).
  • Incumbent Status: No incumbent for this configuration. Ken Calvert (R), who held the old 41st, is running in the new CA-40. Linda Sánchez (D), in Congress since 2003 and currently representing CA-38, is running here instead.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): June 2 top-two primary (official Statement of Vote): Linda Sánchez (D) 37.5%, Mitch Clemmons (R) 35.8%, Hector De La Torre (D) 13.9%, Shonique Williams (D) 12.8%. November ballot (top-two system, per the certified June 2 Statement of Vote): Linda Sánchez (D) and Mitch Clemmons (R); write-in candidates not listed. Sánchez beat former Assemblymember De La Torre, who had challenged her campaign-finance practices, for the Democratic slot (Ballotpedia News).

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Linda Sánchez (D), a 12-term member and ranking Democrat on the Ways and Means trade subcommittee, faces Mitch Clemmons (R), a plumbing contractor and 2022 State Senate candidate.
  • Voting History: Redrawn district. Sánchez won the old CA-38 59.8% to 40.2% over Eric Ching (R) in 2024 (+19.6) and 58.1% to 41.9% over Ching in 2022 (+16.2). Calvert won the old CA-41 51.7% to 48.3% in 2024.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: The Republican vote consolidated behind one candidate while Democrats split three ways, so Clemmons ran close in the primary; combined Democratic support was about 64%. Cost of living, housing and healthcare access in working-class, majority-Latino Gateway Cities dominate; Sánchez campaigns on healthcare equity and childcare affordability, Clemmons on border security, lower taxes and deregulation (Smarter.vote).
  • National Alignment: Sánchez is a leading Democratic critic of Trump's tariffs: as trade subcommittee ranking member she introduced the Stopping a Rogue President on Trade Act (April 2025) to scrap the baseline tariffs and require congressional approval for new ones (Ways and Means Democrats). Clemmons backs secure borders, the SAVE Act and proof of citizenship for voting.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid D (as of Sept 25); not on Inside Elections' (Oct 1) or Sabato's (Sept 29) competitive lists (i.e. safe). No public poll was found as of 3 October. Sánchez had raised $1.60M with $416,000 cash on hand at June 30 (FEC); no significant Clemmons fundraising found.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Sánchez, as ranking Democrat on the Ways and Means trade subcommittee, is a key voice on tariff and trade-agreement legislation affecting US–India trade. No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026; her official caucus list does not include the India Caucus.

CA-45.title: California District 45 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Diverse north and west Orange County seat — Westminster, Garden Grove and Fountain Valley (the heart of Little Saigon), plus Cypress, Buena Park and Brea — with Cerritos, Artesia and part of Lakewood in Los Angeles County; Asian Americans, largely Vietnamese American, are a key bloc. Proposition 50 added more Democratic LA County areas, moving it from about Harris +1.5 to Harris +4 on 2024 presidential results (Inside Elections).
  • Incumbent Status: Derek Tran (D), elected in 2024 by unseating Michelle Steel; running for a second term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): June 2 top-two primary (official Statement of Vote): Derek Tran (D) 53.8%, Chuong V. Vo (R) 15.3%, Chi "Charlie" Nguyen (R) 11.8%, Tom Vo (R) 8.5%, Mark Leonard (R) 5.9%, Amy Phan West (R) 4.7%. Tran, the only Democrat, took a majority against five Republicans, who combined for about 46%. November ballot (top-two system, per the certified June 2 Statement of Vote): Derek Tran (D) and Chuong Vo (R); write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Derek Tran (D), an Army Reserve veteran, lawyer and son of Vietnamese refugees who sits on the Armed Services Committee, faces Chuong Vo (R), a retired Torrance police officer and Cerritos city councilmember (2020–25) running on public safety and costs (Ballotpedia News).
  • Voting History: Tran beat Michelle Steel (R) 50.1% to 49.9% in 2024 (a 596-vote margin, +0.2); Steel had won 52.4% to 47.6% over Jay Chen (D) in 2022 (+4.8). Both results were under the pre-2026 lines.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Vietnamese American voters, historically Republican-leaning and anti-communist, are pivotal, and both nominees are Vietnamese American. Cost of living and public safety lead Vo's message, while immigration enforcement weighs on the district's large immigrant communities.
  • National Alignment: Tran positions as a centrist: he backs immigration reform combining technology-based border security with pathways to citizenship, but broke with most Democrats in 2025 to vote for the Laken Riley Act, drawing criticism from immigrant-rights groups (Wikipedia). Vo runs as a law-and-order Republican focused on public safety, lowering costs and government accountability.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Likely D (as of Sept 25); Inside Elections Likely D (Oct 1); Sabato Likely D (Sept 29). No independent public poll was found as of 3 October. As of June 30, Tran had raised $4.98M to Vo's $496,000 (Ballotpedia News).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026. Tran sits on the House Armed Services Committee and co-chairs the Congressional Caucus on Vietnam, giving him a role in Indo-Pacific defence policy.

CA-48.title: California District 48 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Inland seat spanning East and North County San Diego (including Escondido, Poway and Santee) and parts of Riverside County, now including Palm Springs. Proposition 50 swung it about 18 points: Trump won 56% to 41% under the old lines, while Harris would have won the new district 50% to 47% (Ballotpedia News); Cook puts its PVI at D+2, and Democratic registration is now 37% against 33% Republican.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Darrell Issa (R), the veteran Republican incumbent, is retiring at the end of his term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): June 2 top-two primary (official Statement of Vote): Jim Desmond (R) 38.9%, Marni von Wilpert (D) 20.8%, Ammar Campa-Najjar (D) 10.6%, Kevin Patrick O'Neil (R) 6.9%, Brandon Riker (D) 6.3%; seven other candidates shared the rest. Across the official count, Democratic candidates combined for 53.2% and Republicans 45.8%. November ballot (top-two system, per the certified June 2 Statement of Vote): Jim Desmond (R) and Marni von Wilpert (D); write-in candidates not listed. Desmond switched to this seat after Issa announced his retirement (CalMatters).

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Jim Desmond (R), a San Diego County supervisor and former San Marcos mayor, faces Marni von Wilpert (D), a San Diego city councilmember who flipped a historically Republican council district.
  • Voting History: Redrawn district. Issa won the old CA-48 59.3% to 40.7% over Stephen Houlahan (D) in 2024 (+18.6) and 60.4% to 39.6% over Houlahan in 2022 (+20.8).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Housing affordability is central: von Wilpert pitches housing expansion by cutting regulatory barriers, while Desmond campaigns on lowering taxes, deregulation and controlling state-imposed costs (Ballotpedia News). The addition of Democratic-leaning Palm Springs to the district's San Diego County Republican base is the key structural change.
  • National Alignment: Von Wilpert runs against Trump administration policies, particularly immigration enforcement and tariffs. Desmond stresses his local-government record and conservative fiscal message on taxes and regulation.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Lean D (as of Sept 25); Inside Elections Tilt D (as of Oct 1); Sabato Leans D (as of Sept 29). No independent public poll was found as of 3 October. CalMatters (Sept 29) reports Desmond holds a significant cash advantage after von Wilpert's contested Democratic primary; FEC figures could not be confirmed for this brief.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

CO-05.title: Colorado District 5 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Colorado's 5th District covers most of El Paso County — Colorado Springs and its suburbs — home to five military installations (Peterson and Schriever Space Force Bases, Fort Carson, the Air Force Academy, Cheyenne Mountain) and more than 100,000 veterans. Trump carried it 53.2% to 44.1% in 2024 (+9.1); Cook PVI R+5. Not redrawn for 2026. Unaffiliated voters outnumber registered Republicans, who in turn outnumber Democrats roughly two to one.
  • Incumbent Status: Rep. Jeff Crank (R), a former radio host and Americans for Prosperity executive, first elected in 2024; running for a second term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Jessica Killin 61.2%, Joe Reagan 38.8%; Republicans — Crank unopposed, in the June 30, 2026 primary. November ballot (Colorado Secretary of State official candidate list, updated Sept 15): Jeff Crank (R), Jessica Killin (D), Christopher Mitchell (American Constitution) and Mark Elworth (Libertarian), plus unaffiliated write-in candidate Steven Fuller. The July pre-certification field was reported by Ballotpedia.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Freshman Jeff Crank (R) faces Jessica Killin (D), a Colorado Springs native, Army military police veteran, former USAA executive and ex-chief of staff to Second Gentleman Doug Emhoff. No Democrat has ever won the seat since its creation in 1972.
  • Voting History: Crank won the open seat in 2024, 54.7% to 40.9% over River Gassen (+13.8). In 2022 Doug Lamborn (R) won 56.0% to 40.3% over David Torres (+15.7).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: The military economy dominates: U.S. Space Command headquarters is moving in phases from Colorado Springs to Huntsville, Alabama after Trump's 2025 decision, a sore point for local leaders. Housing affordability, VA clinic quality and the regulation of data centres also featured in the August 27 debate.
  • National Alignment: Crank defends the Iran operations ("I'm not going to vote to pull the rug out from underneath our men and women who are deployed") and campaigns on the 2025 tax law's tip and tax cuts. Killin wants Congress to assert War Powers authority over Iran, opposes tariffs, attacks the tax law for adding $5 trillion to the debt and for Medicaid cuts, and backs a ban on congressional stock trading.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings have moved toward Democrats — Cook Lean R (moved from Likely R; as of Sept 25), Inside Elections Tilt R (moved from Lean R on Sept 22; unchanged as of Oct 1), Sabato Leans R (moved from Likely R on Sept 16; unchanged as of Sept 29). No independent public poll found; a Democratic internal poll by Global Strategy Group (July 16–21) had Crank 45%, Killin 44%. At June 30 Killin had raised $3.14M with $1.59M cash on hand; Crank had raised $2.18M with $1.47M on hand.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

CO-08.title: Colorado District 8 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Colorado's 8th District runs north along Interstate 25 from Denver's northern suburbs (Adams County, Thornton, Northglenn, Westminster) through parts of Larimer and Weld counties to Greeley; created in 2021 after Colorado gained a seat in reapportionment. Trump carried it by about 1.8 points in 2024; Cook PVI EVEN. Not redrawn for 2026. Registration at Sept 1: 241,258 unaffiliated, 110,630 Democrats, 101,876 Republicans.
  • Incumbent Status: Rep. Gabe Evans (R), a former state legislator, police officer, Army veteran and Weld County farmer, first elected in 2024; running for a second term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Manny Rutinel 62.8%, Shannon Bird 32.5%, Evan Munsing 4.6%; Republicans — Evans unopposed, in the June 30, 2026 primary. November ballot (Colorado Secretary of State official candidate list, updated Sept 15): Gabe Evans (R), Manny Rutinel (D) and Dave Wood (Libertarian); no write-in candidates listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Gabe Evans (R) faces Manny Rutinel (D), 31, a former state representative and Army Corps of Engineers economist who resigned his legislative seat to campaign full-time and is running as a progressive refusing corporate PAC money.
  • Voting History: Evans unseated Yadira Caraveo (D) in 2024, 48.9% to 48.2% (+0.7). Caraveo had won the new seat in 2022, 48.4% to 47.7% over Barbara Kirkmeyer (+0.7).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Cost of living and health premiums after the lapse of enhanced ACA credits are Rutinel's central attack; Evans stresses "all-of-the-above" energy and deregulation in a district with heavy Weld County oil and gas production (Colorado Politics). Immigration enforcement is sharply contested: Rutinel attacks "masked agents in unmarked cars", while Evans says detention should prioritise violent criminals.
  • National Alignment: Evans runs on bipartisan credentials (Problem Solvers Caucus; seven bills passed with bipartisan support), border security with "more effective legal pathways", and energy deregulation. Rutinel pledges to "fight the corrupt Trump-Evans tariffs", blames Evans for expired ACA subsidies, backs a congressional stock-trading ban and a path to citizenship for Dreamers.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Toss Up (Sept 25); Inside Elections Toss-up (Oct 1); Sabato Toss-up (Sept 29). A McLaughlin & Associates poll for Enhancing American Competitiveness, a conservative group backing Evans (Sept 16–17, 400 LV), had Evans 48%, Rutinel 46%, with Trump's district approval at 34% and the generic ballot tied 47–47. At June 30 Evans had raised $5.39M with $3.88M cash on hand; Rutinel had raised $4.34M with $0.60M on hand after the primary.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

FL-14.title: Florida District 14 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: FL-14 — Tampa Bay: South Tampa, Town 'N' Country and Riverview out to the Polk and Manatee county lines. Florida's May 2026 mid-decade redistricting removed Democratic St. Petersburg and added rural Hillsborough, swinging the seat about 19 points to roughly Trump +10.
  • Incumbent Status: Kathy Castor (D), in Congress since 2007 and a ten-time winner, seeking re-election in much less friendly territory.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Castor renominated; Republicans — Mike Beltran won an eight-way primary on August 18 over State Rep. Kevin Steele and former Trump aide Bea Valenti, among others. November ballot (certified): Kathy Castor (D), Mike Beltran (R), Brian Lambert (Libertarian); write-in candidates Salomon Hernandez Sr. and Keith Varian.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Kathy Castor (D), a senior Energy and Commerce member known for climate and healthcare work, faces Mike Beltran (R), a Harvard-trained attorney who served in the Florida House from 2018 to 2024.
  • Voting History: On the old lines Castor won easily — 57.0% to 41.6% over Rocky Rochford in 2024 (+15.4) and 56.9% to 43.1% in 2022 (+13.8) — but those results came in a district Harris carried; the new seat backed Trump by double digits.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Hurricane recovery and soaring property-insurance premiums, housing costs and electricity bills dominate in a storm-battered Tampa Bay; the legitimacy of the new map, still being litigated on the merits, is a Democratic talking point.
  • National Alignment: Castor runs on local cost of living — housing, power bills, groceries and healthcare — and her seniority; Beltran ties her to national Democrats and runs on the Republican agenda of tax cuts and public safety in a seat drawn for his party.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Inside Elections rates it a Toss Up (Oct 1), as do Cook (Sept 25) and Sabato (Sept 29); Inside Elections calls it the fight of Castor's political life. Castor's name recognition and incumbency offset the new lines; Republican groups have outspent Democratic ones on the race so far.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

FL-20.title: Florida District 20 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: FL-20 — central and northern Broward County; about 48% Black and one of Florida's safest Democratic seats, created in 1992 as a Black-opportunity district. Wasserman Schultz moved here after the May 2026 map made her old seat Republican-leaning. (Listed in the seat sheet as FL-25.)
  • Incumbent Status: Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D), in Congress since 2005 and former DNC chair, running in a district she has not previously represented.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Wasserman Schultz about 45%, Holness 23%, with the rest split among three other Black candidates, in the August 18 primary; Republicans — Brent Andersen won the nomination the same day. November ballot (certified): Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D), Brent Andersen (R), Kedner Maxime (independent); no write-in candidate qualified.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D), a senior Appropriations member and chair of the House Democratic Steering Committee, faces Brent Andersen (R) in a seat where the Democratic primary was the decisive contest.
  • Voting History: In her old FL-25 she won 54.5% to 45.5% over Chris Eddy in 2024 (+9.0) and 55.1% to 44.9% over Carla Spalding in 2022 (+10.2); FL-20 itself has long returned Democrats by wide margins.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Representation is the flashpoint: Broward's Black Democratic leaders objected to a non-Black incumbent who lives outside the district winning a fractured primary in a Voting Rights Act seat. Housing costs and insurance premiums are the main kitchen-table issues.
  • National Alignment: Wasserman Schultz runs on her appropriations clout, healthcare and opposition to the Trump agenda and the DeSantis map; Republicans frame her as a carpetbagger in a district that has long returned Democrats by wide margins.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook rates it Solid D (Sept 25); it is not on Inside Elections’ or Sabato’s competitive lists (i.e. safe). The open question is lingering resentment among Black voters and any spillover into turnout for statewide races.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

FL-23.title: Florida District 23 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: FL-23 — Palm Beach County. Florida's May 2026 redistricting turned Frankel's old FL-22 Republican-leaning, so she moved to the redrawn 23rd, which Cook rates as favouring Democrats. (Listed in the seat sheet as FL-22.)
  • Incumbent Status: Lois Frankel (D), in Congress since 2013 and a former West Palm Beach mayor, seeking re-election in the renumbered seat.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Frankel 75%, Doyle 23%; Republicans — Deborah Adeimy beat Paola Branda in the August 18 primaries. November ballot: Lois Frankel (D) and Deborah Adeimy (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Lois Frankel (D), 78, an Appropriations veteran and the first woman to lead Democrats in the Florida House, faces Deborah Adeimy (R), who beat Paola Branda for the Republican nomination.
  • Voting History: On her old lines Frankel twice beat Dan Franzese — 55.0% to 45.0% in 2024 (+10) and 55.1% to 44.9% in 2022 (+10).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Housing costs and property insurance top voter concerns in coastal Palm Beach County; the area's large retiree and Jewish communities make Social Security, Medicare and US–Israel policy salient.
  • National Alignment: Frankel runs on pragmatic healthcare gains such as the $35 insulin cap, abortion rights and strong security assistance to Israel; Adeimy runs on the Republican agenda of lower taxes, border security and support for Trump.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook rates it Solid D (Sept 25); it is not on Inside Elections’ or Sabato’s competitive lists (i.e. safe). The competitive contest is now in her old FL-22, which is Republican-leaning. No public general-election poll had been identified as of 3 October.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

FL-25.title: Florida District 25 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: FL-25 — a redrawn coastal strip from Palm Beach County through Broward to northern Miami-Dade; about Trump +10, one of four Democratic seats the May 2026 map targeted. Moskowitz moved here after his FL-23 was dismantled. (Listed in the seat sheet as FL-23.)
  • Incumbent Status: Jared Moskowitz (D), two terms since 2023, running in the renumbered seat.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Moskowitz 64%, Larkin 36% (a DSA-backed organiser); Republicans — former Boca Raton mayor Scott Singer won; both primaries were held on August 18. November ballot: Jared Moskowitz (D) and Scott Singer (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Jared Moskowitz (D), a Parkland native and DeSantis's former emergency-management chief known for bipartisanship, faces Scott Singer (R), former mayor of Boca Raton.
  • Voting History: On his old lines Moskowitz won narrowly — 52.3% to 47.7% over Joe Kaufman in 2024 (+4.6) and 51.6% to 46.8% over Joe Budd in 2022 (+4.8) — in a seat friendlier than the new one.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Property-insurance and condo-assessment costs, hurricane preparedness and housing affordability lead in coastal South Florida; gun safety resonates in the Parkland area, and the large Jewish electorate keeps Israel policy prominent.
  • National Alignment: Moskowitz runs as an independent-minded centrist — he joined the House DOGE caucus and backs Israel strongly; Singer ties him to national Democrats and runs on taxes, public safety and the new map's Republican tilt.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook (Sept 25), Inside Elections (Oct 1) and Sabato (Sept 29) all rate it a Toss Up, and press coverage describes a Toss Up that could decide the House majority; Moskowitz's crossover appeal is tested against a Trump +10 electorate. No public general-election poll had been identified as of 3 October.

Gov-AK.title: Alaska (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Alaska Governor — open seat in a Republican-leaning state that uses a top-four primary and ranked-choice general election. Cook and Sabato now rate it a Toss Up — not the Safe R in the seat sheet.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R), in office since 2018, is term-limited.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): In the August 18, 2026 top-four primary, Kreiss-Tomkins (D) 22.5%, Begich (D) 20.8%, Wilson (R) 10.0%, Bronson (R) 8.1%; Begich then withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, and fifth-placed Treg Taylor (R, 7.3%), reinstated on September 4 after an earlier disqualification, took the vacated finalist spot. November ballot (certified, Alaska Division of Elections candidate list): Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D), Dave Bronson (R), Treg Taylor (R) and Bernadette Wilson (R), plus certified write-in James Parkin (R); the general election uses ranked-choice voting.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D), a former state representative (2013–2023), faces three Republicans: businesswoman Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage mayor Dave Bronson and former attorney general Treg Taylor.
  • Voting History: Dunleavy won outright with 50.3% in a four-way race in 2022, and 51.4% to 44.4% over Mark Begich in 2018 (+7.0).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: The size of the Permanent Fund Dividend, the state budget and oil revenue, school funding, and high fuel and grocery costs — diesel topped $6.60 a gallon in September.
  • National Alignment: Kreiss-Tomkins runs on affordability, education funding and fiscal stability; the Republicans split between establishment and Trump-aligned lanes, with Wilson urging rivals to drop out to avoid splitting the vote.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook rates the race Toss Up (Oct 1); Inside Elections Lean R (Sept 3) and Sabato Toss-up (Sept 3), per Wikipedia's ratings table. An AARP poll (Sept 8–11; bipartisan, by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research; 800 likely voters) has Kreiss-Tomkins at 40% in the first round and winning 50% to 40% after ranked-choice tabulation, but 18% are undecided and lean heavily toward Trump.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026. Alaska's LNG export ambitions are relevant to Asian energy buyers.

sections.heading: Key Local Media
sections.html:
• Anchorage Daily News (adn.com) — State's largest newspaper
  • Alaska Beacon (alaskabeacon.com) — Nonprofit statehouse and campaign reporting
  • Alaska Public Media (alaskapublic.org) — Statewide public radio and TV
  • Alaska Survey Research (alaskasurveyresearch.com) — Anchorage pollster; ranked-choice simulations

Gov-AL.title: Alabama (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Alabama Governor — open seat in a deeply Republican state. Rated Solid/Safe R by Cook, Inside Elections and Sabato.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Gov. Kay Ivey (R), in office since 2017, is term-limited.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Tuberville 85.4%, McFeeters 9.6%, Santivasci 5.0%; Democrats — Jones 78.6%, Boyd 9.7%, others under 6% in the May 19 primaries. November ballot: Tommy Tuberville (R) and Doug Jones (D), with no third-party or independent candidate listed; write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R), the former Auburn football coach elected to the Senate in 2020, faces former Sen. Doug Jones (D), the ex-federal prosecutor he unseated — a rematch of 2020.
  • Voting History: Ivey won 67.4% to 29.2% over Yolanda Flowers in 2022 (+38.2) and 59.5% to 40.4% over Walt Maddox in 2018 (+19.1).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Rural hospital closures and Medicaid non-expansion, prison conditions under federal scrutiny, and education and workforce needs for the state's auto and aerospace industries.
  • National Alignment: Tuberville runs as a Trump-aligned conservative on taxes, crime and cultural issues; Jones runs on healthcare access, Medicaid expansion and competent government.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook rates it Solid R (Oct 1); Inside Elections Solid R and Sabato Safe R (both Sept 3). A yes. every kid. poll (July 8–11) had Tuberville 49%, Jones 41%. Tuberville had raised $14.5M with $5.2M on hand at August 31, against Jones's $4.8M and $2.5M.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Gov-AR.title: Arkansas (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Arkansas Governor — a deeply Republican state (Trump +31 in 2024).
  • Incumbent Status: Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), first term since January 2023 and Trump-endorsed, seeking re-election.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Sanders unopposed; Democrats — Love 81.0%, Xayprasith-Mays 19.0% in the March 3, 2026 primary. November ballot: Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), Fredrick Love (D) and Colt Shelby (Libertarian), per Wikipedia's race page; not confirmed against the Arkansas Secretary of State's certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), Trump's former White House press secretary and daughter of ex-Gov. Mike Huckabee, faces Fredrick Love (D), a state senator from Little Rock since 2023.
  • Voting History: Sanders won 63.0% to 35.2% over Chris Jones in 2022 (+27.8); Asa Hutchinson won 65.3% to 31.8% in 2018 (+33.5).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Sanders's LEARNS Act school-voucher and teacher-pay overhaul, income-tax cuts, a planned new prison, and rural hospital strain.
  • National Alignment: Sanders runs as a national conservative figure on education choice, tax cuts and culture-war issues; Love runs on public schools, healthcare and kitchen-table costs.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid R (Oct 1); Inside Elections Solid R (Aug 6); Sabato Safe R (Aug 26). A Hendrix College poll (Aug 11–12) had Sanders at 45% to Love's 40%, with 7% for Shelby — a narrower margin than the state's 2024 presidential result.

Gov-AZ.title: Arizona (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Arizona Governor — a purple state Trump carried by 5.5 points in 2024, with a Republican legislature. Rated Lean D by Cook and Sabato and Toss-up by Inside Elections (see Race Outlook).
  • Incumbent Status: Katie Hobbs (D), first term since January 2023, seeking re-election.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Hobbs unopposed; Republicans — Rep. Andy Biggs won the July 21 primary with 74.0%, defeating Rep. David Schweikert (about 14%) and Scott Neely (about 7%); Karrin Taylor Robson had suspended her campaign in February. November ballot: Katie Hobbs (D) and Andy Biggs (R); the August HighGround poll also tested Teri Ann Hourigan (No Labels) and Risa Lombardo (Green), but third-party/independent candidates were not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Katie Hobbs (D), a former social worker and secretary of state, faces Andy Biggs (R), a Freedom Caucus congressman and former chair of the group.
  • Voting History: Hobbs beat Kari Lake 50.3% to 49.6% in 2022 (+0.7); Republican Doug Ducey won 56.0% to 41.8% in 2018 (+14.2).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Water supply and Colorado River cuts, housing costs, border security, and Hobbs's record number of vetoes against the Republican legislature.
  • National Alignment: Hobbs runs as a pragmatic check on the legislature, on affordability, abortion rights and border funding; Biggs runs as a hard-line Trump ally on immigration, election integrity and tax cuts.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Lean D (Oct 1); Inside Elections Toss-up (Aug 6); Sabato Leans D (Aug 26). A HighGround poll (Aug 15–18) has Hobbs 49.5%, Biggs 34.3%, with independents breaking 55% to 19% for Hobbs; she has also outspent Biggs on advertising.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026. Arizona's semiconductor buildout (TSMC, Intel) links it to US–India chip supply-chain cooperation.

Gov-CA.title: California (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: California — governorship; the most populous state and a Democratic stronghold that Harris carried by about 20 points (58.5% to 38.3%) in 2024. Republicans have not won a gubernatorial race since 2006. Statewide races use a top-two primary in which all candidates appear on a single ballot.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), in office since January 2019, is term-limited.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Top-two primary, June 2, 2026 (61 candidates; certified Statement of Vote): Xavier Becerra (D) 28.0%, Steve Hilton (R) 24.6%, Tom Steyer (D) 22.8%, Chad Bianco (R) 10.2%, Katie Porter (D) 4.4%, Matt Mahan (D) 3.5%. Becerra and Hilton advanced. November ballot (top-two system, per the certified June 2 Statement of Vote): Xavier Becerra (D) and Steve Hilton (R); write-in candidates not listed. Rep. Eric Swalwell (D), an early frontrunner, suspended his campaign on April 12 after sexual-misconduct allegations, which he denies, and resigned from Congress effective April 14.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Xavier Becerra (D), former HHS Secretary under Biden, state attorney general and 12-term congressman, faces Steve Hilton (R), a former Downing Street adviser to David Cameron and ex-Fox News host, endorsed by Trump.
  • Voting History: Newsom won 59.2% to 40.8% over Brian Dahle (R) in 2022 (+18.4), after defeating John Cox (R) 61.9% to 38.1% in 2018 (+23.9).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Cost of living dominates: 65% of likely voters call affordability 'very important' to their vote (PPIC, Sept 2026). Housing and homelessness — Hilton proposes ten new cities and building on undeveloped land; Becerra pledges to cut red tape and expand down-payment aid. Energy and gas prices — Hilton would expand in-state oil drilling; Becerra would let communities limit AI data centres (CalMatters debate report).
  • National Alignment: Becerra runs squarely against Trump, invoking him repeatedly in the 30 September CNN debate, attacking Hilton's deportation stance, and pledging to backfill coverage lost to federal Medicaid cuts (CalMatters). Hilton, Trump-endorsed, has called the deportation campaign 'perfect' but runs ads inviting Trump opponents to back him; he would abolish state income tax on the first $150,000 of earnings and replace part of Medi-Cal with health spending accounts.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid D (as of Oct 1); Inside Elections Solid D (as of Sept 17); Sabato Safe D (as of Sept 29). The PPIC Statewide Survey (Sept 4–10) has Becerra leading 60% to 38% among likely voters; the Berkeley IGS poll (released Sept 24) has him ahead 58% to 33%. At June 30 Becerra had over $6.2M cash on hand to Hilton's $2.1M (with $1.4M in unpaid bills); between July 1 and the report's Aug 22 publication Becerra had raised $6M in large donations to Hilton's $1.2M (Stocktonia/CalMatters, Aug 22).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: California has the largest Indian-American population of any state: 830,259 (2.1%) in the 2020 Census, concentrated in the Bay Area tech sector, where H-1B policy is a live issue. No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

  • PPIC Statewide Survey (ppic.org) — Independent, nonpartisan pollster; regular likely-voter surveys
  • Berkeley IGS Poll (igs.berkeley.edu) — UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies; large-sample statewide polls

Gov-CO.title: Colorado (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Colorado — governorship; a former swing state now firmly Democratic-leaning, which Harris carried by 11 points (54.1% to 43.1%) in 2024. Republicans have not won the governorship since 2002, and Democrats hold near-supermajorities in the legislature.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Gov. Jared Polis (D), in office since January 2019, is term-limited.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Attorney General Phil Weiser upset Sen. Michael Bennet, winning 56.7% despite being heavily outspent by a pro-Bennet super PAC (Colorado Sun). Republicans — Victor Marx 39.9%, state Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer 39.4%, state Rep. Scott Bottoms 21%; Marx won by about 2,500 votes, outside the automatic-recount threshold, with the result confirmed on July 9 (Colorado Sun). Primary held June 30, 2026. November ballot (Colorado Secretary of State official candidate list, updated Sept 15): Phil Weiser (D), Victor Marx (R), Stephen T. Hamilton (American Constitution), Eric Mulder (Libertarian), Jeff Peckman (Unity), Erik Underwood (Approval Voting) and Greg Lopez (unaffiliated); write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Phil Weiser (D), two-term attorney general known for suing the Trump administration, faces Victor Marx (R), a Marine veteran and evangelical ministry founder with no prior office. Former Republican congressman Greg Lopez is running as an unaffiliated candidate; four minor-party candidates are also on the ballot.
  • Voting History: Polis won 58.5% to 39.2% over Heidi Ganahl (R) in 2022 (+19.3), after defeating Walker Stapleton (R) 53.4% to 42.8% in 2018 (+10.6).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Housing affordability is voters' top concern: Weiser pledges 40,000 affordable starter homes, Marx favours faster housing approvals and fee reviews, and Lopez proposes a 'Starter Homes' initiative (Colorado Politics). The state faces a $1.5 billion budget shortfall; Weiser argues for reform of the TABOR tax-limitation amendment, while Marx rules out new taxes or fees. Debates are a running dispute: Marx demanded an unmoderated format and the only scheduled debate was called off (CPR News).
  • National Alignment: Weiser runs on his record of litigation against the Trump administration and on affordability, and attacked Bennet in the primary for voting to confirm Trump appointees. Marx, close to Turning Point USA circles, wants state cooperation with ICE despite Colorado law limiting it, opposes sanctuary policies and proposes a 'Border-Related Crime Strike Force'. Neither has published detailed positions on tariffs or the Iran war.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid D (as of Oct 1); Inside Elections Solid D (as of Sept 17); Sabato Safe D (as of Sept 29). No independent public general-election poll found. As of July 27 Weiser had $369,303 cash on hand to Marx's $136,989; Marx spent more ($221,627) than he raised ($185,694) in the June–July period (Colorado Newsline, Aug 5).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Colorado's Indian-American population was 34,400 (0.6%) in the 2020 Census. No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Gov-CT.title: Connecticut (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Connecticut — governorship; a reliably Democratic New England state that Harris carried by about 14.5 points (56.4% to 41.9%) in 2024, with a wealthy Fairfield County suburban belt and high cost-of-living and energy-price pressures.
  • Incumbent Status: Gov. Ned Lamont (D), in office since January 2019, is running for a third term with Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz as running mate.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Lamont 68%, state Rep. Josh Elliott 32% in the August 11 primary, Lamont's first primary challenge as governor; he won all but three towns (CBIA; CT Mirror). Republicans — state Sen. Ryan Fazio won about 92% of delegates at the May 16 convention; Betsy McCaughey fell short of the 15% threshold, so no Republican primary was held. November ballot: Ned Lamont (D) and Ryan Fazio (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Two-term Gov. Ned Lamont (D), a self-funding businessman, faces state Sen. Ryan Fazio (R) of Greenwich, a 36-year-old financial adviser with a commodities-industry background, running on tax and energy-cost relief.
  • Voting History: Lamont won 56.0% to 43.1% over Bob Stefanowski (R) in 2022 (+12.9), after a narrow 2018 win over Stefanowski, 49.4% to 46.2% (+3.2).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Cost of living is the top issue (27%), followed by the economy (23%) and taxes (11%) in the Quinnipiac poll of Sept 8–14. Fazio proposes a 1.5-point income-tax cut for middle earners and a property-tax cap of 2% or inflation, and has campaigned on electricity bills after co-authoring legislation to itemise and cut 'public benefits' charges. Fazio is the first major-party gubernatorial nominee since 2014 to use the Citizens' Election Program, receiving $18 million in public financing (WSHU).
  • National Alignment: Lamont opposes Trump's immigration policies, tariffs and the Iran strikes but pitches pragmatic management: 'We're fighting Trump where we've got to fight him... we got to manage the state every day.' Fazio has said he voted for Trump in all three elections; Quinnipiac finds Fazio ahead on taxes (72–22) and immigration (63–36), Lamont on healthcare (83–15) and cost of living (63–29).

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid D (as of Oct 1); Inside Elections Solid D (as of Sept 17); Sabato Safe D (as of Sept 29). Quinnipiac (Sept 8–14, 1,288 likely voters) has Lamont leading 55% to 38%, with Lamont's approval at 50%; Sacred Heart University/WFSB/CT Insider (Sept 1–8, registered voters) has him ahead 48.2% to 33.9%. Lamont had put more than $10 million of his own money into the race by mid-September; Fazio received $18 million in public financing (WSHU, Sept 16).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Connecticut's Indian-American population was 60,634 (1.68%) in the 2020 Census. No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Gov-FL.title: Florida (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Florida Governor — open seat in a state that has moved firmly Republican (Trump +13 in 2024). Forecasters rate it Lean R to Likely R (see Race Outlook).
  • Incumbent Status: None. Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), in office since 2019, is term-limited.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Donalds 47.8%, Collins 25.2%, Fishback 10.5%, Renner 8.5%; Democrats — Jolly 61.0%, Foster 15.1%, Joseph 9.6% in the August 18 primaries. November ballot (certified): Byron Donalds (R), David Jolly (D), Scott Jewett (Libertarian), and no-party candidates Dean Abrams, Charles Burkett, Jeffrey Peter “Dr. Jeff” Datto, Moliere Dimanche and Frank J. Russo; write-in candidates Kathy Anderson and Erik Morris.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Rep. Byron Donalds (R), a Trump-endorsed congressman from southwest Florida since 2021, faces David Jolly (D), a former Republican congressman (2014–2017) who switched parties, with ex-Rep. Gwen Graham as his running mate.
  • Voting History: DeSantis won 59.4% to 40.0% over Charlie Crist in 2022 (+19.4) after edging Andrew Gillum 49.6% to 49.2% in 2018 (+0.4).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Florida's property-insurance crisis, condominium safety assessments, housing affordability, hurricane recovery and the state's new congressional map dominate.
  • National Alignment: Donalds runs as a Trump loyalist promising to extend DeSantis's agenda on taxes, education and immigration; Jolly runs as an anti-extremism moderate focused on insurance costs and housing.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook rates it Lean R (Oct 1); Inside Elections Likely R (Sept 3); Sabato Likely R (Aug 26). Summer polls had Donalds ahead — University of North Florida (July 8–17) 46% to 41% and Targoz Market Research (July 20–26) 45% to 38% — while a Democratic-sponsored Hart Research poll (Aug 10–13) had Jolly 46%, Donalds 45%. Donalds had raised $13.8M as of August 13.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Gov-GA.title: Georgia (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Georgia Governor — open seat in a Sun Belt swing state Trump carried by 2.2 points in 2024. Rated a Toss Up by Cook, Inside Elections and Sabato — not the Safe R in the seat sheet.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Gov. Brian Kemp (R), in office since 2019, is term-limited.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Burt Jones 38.4%, Rick Jackson 32.5%, Brad Raffensperger 15.0%, Chris Carr 11.9% on May 19, then Jackson beat Trump-backed Lt. Gov. Burt Jones 52.6% to 47.4% in the June 16 runoff; Democrats — Bottoms 56.2%, Esteves 18.7%, Thurmond 12.9%, Duncan 7.0% on May 19. November ballot: Rick Jackson (R), Keisha Lance Bottoms (D), Chase Oliver (Libertarian); write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Rick Jackson (R), a healthcare executive who entered in February and has largely self-funded his campaign, faces Keisha Lance Bottoms (D), former Atlanta mayor and Biden White House official, who would be Georgia's first woman and first Black governor.
  • Voting History: Kemp beat Stacey Abrams 53.4% to 45.9% in 2022 (+7.5) after a 50.2% to 48.8% win over her in 2018 (+1.4). Democrats have not won the governorship since 1998.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Health costs after ACA premiums more than doubled, housing, the economy of metro Atlanta, and election administration. Democratic primary turnout exceeded Republican turnout for the first time since 2006.
  • National Alignment: Jackson runs as a businessman-outsider on taxes, crime and healthcare; Bottoms runs on affordability, Medicaid expansion and opposition to Trump-era cuts.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook rates it a Toss Up (Oct 1); Inside Elections Toss-up (Aug 6); Sabato Toss-up (Aug 26). Wikipedia’s polling average as of Sept 24 had Jackson 46.5%, Bottoms 46.3%. Jackson had raised $118.9M (mostly his own money) by July 31 to Bottoms's $5.8M.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Gov-HI.title: Hawaii (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Hawaii — governorship; one of the most Democratic states, which Harris carried by about 23 points (60.6% to 37.5%) in 2024. Republicans have not won the governorship since Linda Lingle's 2006 re-election; the economy rests on tourism and a large military presence.
  • Incumbent Status: Gov. Josh Green (D), a physician in office since December 2022, is running for a second term, with Kauai Mayor Derek Kawakami as his running mate.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Green 81.7%, Lauren Kapoliahi'iaka Shim 5.0%, George Lucas-Tadeo 3.6%, Duke Bourgoin 2.0%; Republicans — Gary Cordery 66.6%, Ken Fujiyama 21.2%, in the August 8, 2026 primary (percentages of all ballots cast, including blanks; Hawaii Public Radio). November ballot: Josh Green (D) and Gary Cordery (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Incumbent Josh Green (D), whose approval ratings are reported at 56% or higher, faces Gary Cordery (R), a contractor and business owner campaigning on tax cuts and housing.
  • Voting History: Green won 63.2% to 36.8% over James 'Duke' Aiona (R) in 2022 (+26.4); in 2018 David Ige (D) defeated Andria Tupola (R) 62.7% to 33.7% (+29.0).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Housing and cost of living: Green declared a housing emergency on taking office and cites tens of thousands of affordable units in the pipeline, while Cordery proposes 15,000 homes priced at $400,000–$600,000 on state land and ending the General Excise Tax on food and medicine (Fox News). Recovery from the 2023 Lahaina wildfire and the March 2026 floods. Green's visitor 'green fee', the first state climate fee, projected to raise about $100 million a year (Civil Beat Q&A).
  • National Alignment: Green says he will work with anyone who helps Hawaii's families but 'stand firm whenever our people or values are threatened', pointing to federal support secured for Maui recovery and the grid; he backs LNG as a bridge fuel to the 2045 renewables target. Cordery runs on fiscal restraint, arguing Hawaii's $20.5 billion budget is excessive; no detailed positions found from either candidate on tariffs, immigration or the Iran war.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid D (as of Oct 1); Inside Elections Solid D (as of Sept 17); Sabato Safe D (as of Sept 29). No public general-election poll found. In reports filed in July (period to June 30), Green had raised $3.5 million since 2022 and held about $2 million cash; Cordery had raised just over $300,000 and reported $14,000 in debt (Hawaii News Now, July 11).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Hawaii's Indian-American population was 2,362 (0.16%) in the 2020 Census. The state hosts US Indo-Pacific Command, the US combatant command responsible for military engagement with India, and the RIMPAC naval exercise in which the Indian Navy participates. No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Gov-IA.title: Iowa (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Iowa Governor — open seat in a farm state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024; forecasters now rate it a possible Democratic gain (see Race Outlook).
  • Incumbent Status: None. Gov. Kim Reynolds (R), in office since 2017, is not seeking re-election.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Lahn 37.7%, Feenstra 36.9%, Steen 14.5%, others under 8%; Democrats — Sand 99.6% in the June 2 primary. November ballot (Iowa Secretary of State candidate list, updated Aug 19): Zach Lahn (R; running mate Derek Wulf), Rob Sand (D; running mate Dave Muhlbauer); no third-party or independent tickets listed (Libertarian Nicholas Gluba was disqualified); write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Zach Lahn (R), a businessman who narrowly beat Rep. Randy Feenstra and has faced scrutiny over time spent in Kansas, faces Rob Sand (D), state auditor since 2019 and a former prosecutor known for high-profile fraud audits.
  • Voting History: Reynolds won 58.0% to 39.5% over Deidre DeJear in 2022 (+18.5) and 50.3% to 47.5% over Fred Hubbell in 2018 (+2.8).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: The farm economy — tariffs, fuel and fertiliser costs amid the Iran war — property taxes, rural hospitals, water quality, and Lahn's residency controversy.
  • National Alignment: Sand runs as a fiscally centrist watchdog appealing to rural voters; Lahn runs as a Trump-aligned conservative on taxes, education choice and agriculture.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings: Cook Lean D (Oct 1); Inside Elections Tilt D (Sept 3) and Sabato Leans D (Sept 3), per Wikipedia's ratings table. Recent public polls: Emerson College (released Sept 3, 750 LV) Sand 49%, Lahn 46%; YouGov (released Sept 11, 2,169 RV) Sand 50%, Lahn 39%; Marist (released Sept 22, 1,050 RV) Sand 54%, Lahn 42%; Fox News (released Oct 1, 1,008 LV) Sand 53%, Lahn 44% (270toWin poll list).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Gov-ID.title: Idaho (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Idaho Governor — one of the most Republican states, where intra-GOP fights between establishment and hard-right wings matter more than the general election. Forecasters rate it Solid/Safe R (see Race Outlook).
  • Incumbent Status: Brad Little (R), in office since 2019, seeking a third term with Trump's endorsement.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Little 59.0%, Fitzpatrick 28.7%; Democrats — Pickens Manweiler 61.4%, Kirkham 17.0%, Durand 14.5% in the May 19, 2026 primary. November ballot (per Wikipedia's race page; not checked against the Idaho Secretary of State's certified list): Brad Little (R), Terri Pickens Manweiler (D), John Stegner (independent) and Paul Sand (Libertarian); write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Brad Little (R), a rancher and former lieutenant governor, faces Terri Pickens Manweiler (D), a Boise attorney and the 2022 Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor, who entered the race in November 2025.
  • Voting History: Little won 60.5% in 2022 against a split field including independent Ammon Bundy, and 59.8% to 38.2% over Paulette Jordan in 2018 (+21.6).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Rapid population growth and housing costs, school funding and a new private-school tax-credit programme (the state teachers' union withdrew its endorsement of Little), and rural healthcare access.
  • National Alignment: Little runs as a mainstream conservative endorsed by Trump and public-safety unions; Pickens runs on public education, healthcare and reproductive rights.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid R (Oct 1); Inside Elections Solid R (Aug 6); Sabato Safe R (Aug 26). A Change Research poll sponsored by Stegner's campaign (July 28–30; 1,213 likely voters) had Little 48%, Pickens Manweiler 27%, Stegner 11%.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Gov-IL.title: Illinois (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Illinois Governor — a solidly Democratic state anchored by Chicago. Rated Solid/Safe D by all major forecasters.
  • Incumbent Status: JB Pritzker (D), in office since 2019, seeking a third term — frequently mentioned as a possible 2028 presidential candidate.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Pritzker unopposed; Republicans — Bailey 53.3%, Dabrowski 28.9%, Mendrick 9.6%, Heidner 8.1% in the March 17 primary. November ballot: JB Pritzker (D), Darren Bailey (R) and Collin Corbett (independent; on the ballot after an objection was withdrawn in June, per Capitol News Illinois); Wikipedia also lists independent Michael Vick, whose ballot status could not be confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October; write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: JB Pritzker (D), a billionaire Hyatt heir and leading Democratic critic of Trump, faces Darren Bailey (R), a downstate farmer and former state senator, Trump-endorsed, in a 2022 rematch.
  • Voting History: Pritzker beat Bailey 54.9% to 42.4% in 2022 (+12.5) and unseated Bruce Rauner 54.5% to 38.8% in 2018 (+15.7).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Federal immigration enforcement and National Guard deployments in Chicago, state pension debt and taxes, crime, and the downstate–Chicago divide.
  • National Alignment: Pritzker runs as a national resistance figure against Trump on immigration, abortion rights and federal cuts; Bailey runs on taxes, crime and rural resentment of Chicago-centred government.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid D (Oct 1); Inside Elections Solid D (Aug 6); Sabato Safe D (Aug 26). A Victory Research poll (Nov 20–24, 2025) had Pritzker 54%, Bailey 34%. The margin will be read as a measure of Pritzker's national standing ahead of 2028.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026. Illinois has one of the largest Indian-American communities in the US.

Gov-KS.title: Kansas (Governor)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Kansas Governor — open seat in a Republican state with a history of electing Democratic governors.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Gov. Laura Kelly (D), in office since 2019, is term-limited.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Masterson 43.2%, Sarnecki 22.4%, Schmidt 13.7%, Schwab 10.9%; Democrats — Holscher 48.6%, Corson 38.8%, Skoog 12.6% in the August 4, 2026 primary. November ballot: Ty Masterson (R) and Cindy Holscher (D); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Ty Masterson (R), Kansas Senate president and Trump-endorsed, faces Cindy Holscher (D), a combative state senator from Johnson County who beat Gov. Kelly's preferred candidate.
  • Voting History: Kelly won narrowly twice — 49.5% to 47.3% over Derek Schmidt in 2022 (+2.2) and 48.0% to 43.0% over Kris Kobach in 2018 (+5.0).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: In Emerson's Sept 15–16 poll, 48% named the economy their top issue, followed by healthcare (14%), threats to democracy and housing affordability (9% each); data-centre expansion and school funding are also live.
  • National Alignment: Masterson runs on lower taxes, safe communities and educational freedom; Holscher runs on public schools, cannabis legalisation and opposing data centres.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
