NM-02.title: New Mexico District 2 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: New Mexico's 2nd District covers the southern half of the state — 15 counties including Las Cruces (Doña Ana), the southern quarter of Albuquerque, the border counties and the Permian Basin oil counties of Eddy and Lea. Trump carried it 50% to 48% in 2024 (about +1.8); Cook PVI EVEN. Not redrawn for 2026 (lines unchanged since the 2021 map).
  • Incumbent Status: Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D), a former Las Cruces city councillor first elected in 2022; running for a third term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Greg Cunningham 84.5%, Jose Orozco 15.5% (Orozco had withdrawn but remained on the ballot); Democrats — Vasquez unopposed, in the June 2, 2026 primary. November ballot: Gabe Vasquez (D) and Greg Cunningham (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Gabe Vasquez (D), 42, faces Greg Cunningham (R), 60, a retired Albuquerque Police detective and Marine combat veteran who worked undercover against cartels and gangs.
  • Voting History: Vasquez won 52.1% to 47.9% in a 2024 rematch with former Rep. Yvette Herrell (R) (+4.2), after unseating her in 2022 by 50.3% to 49.6% (+0.7).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Border security and crime are Cunningham's "wheelhouse"; Vasquez pairs border enforcement with comprehensive immigration reform tied to economic development (Albuquerque Journal). Data-centre development is a live issue: Vasquez backs moratoriums and ratepayer protections, while Cunningham says each community "should be able to decide for itself". Oil and gas in the Permian counties and rising prices also shape the race.
  • National Alignment: Vasquez attacks Trump for "broken promises" on prices, DOGE and tariff refunds, dismisses Trump's proposed $5,000 payment, and criticises the Iran war as a breach of the "no new forever wars" pledge (KOB 4). Cunningham runs on public safety and blames the Biden administration for a border that was "wide open for four years"; Speaker Mike Johnson has campaigned for him. He declined a Spanish-language debate on Univision.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Lean D (Sept 25); Inside Elections Tilt D (Oct 1); Sabato Leans D (Sept 29). An independent SurveyUSA poll for KOB 4 (Aug 28–Sept 2, 554 LV) has Vasquez 46%, Cunningham 43%, with Trump viewed unfavourably by 51% to 39%. In Q2 (to June 30) Cunningham raised nearly $902,000 and Vasquez just under $901,000, but Vasquez held about three times as much cash. Debate on KRQE on October 16.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

sections.html:

  • Source NM (sourcenm.com) — Nonprofit States Newsroom outlet; campaign finance and policy coverage
  • Las Cruces Sun-News (lcsun-news.com) — Daily for Doña Ana County, the district's population centre

NV-01.title: Nevada District 1 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: NV-1 — central and southeast Las Vegas, the Strip, and parts of Henderson; a diverse, heavily Latino and working-class seat built on the hospitality economy. Rated Likely D by Cook and Sabato, Lean D by Inside Elections (see Race Outlook).
  • Incumbent Status: Dina Titus (D), in Congress since 2013 (and earlier 2009–2011), seeking re-election.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Titus 75.9%; Republicans — Carrie Buck 77.7% in the June 9 primary. November ballot: Dina Titus (D) and Carrie Buck (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Dina Titus (D), a former UNLV political science professor and senior Transportation and Infrastructure member, faces Carrie Buck (R), a state senator since 2020 and charter-school leader.
  • Voting History: Titus won 52.0% to 45.3% over Mark Robertson in 2024 (+6.7) and 51.6% to 46.0% over Robertson in 2022 (+5.6) after the 2021 redistricting made the seat more competitive.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: A slide in Las Vegas visitor numbers, led by falling Canadian and Mexican arrivals, threatens casino and hospitality jobs; housing costs and fuel prices compound the strain.
  • National Alignment: Titus runs on protecting hospitality workers, healthcare and Las Vegas's tourism economy; Buck runs on education choice and lower taxes.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Likely D (Sept 25); Inside Elections Lean D (Oct 1); Sabato Likely D (Sept 29). Fundraising was level at about $1.25M raised each in FEC reports as of May 13; no public district poll was found as of 3 October.

NV-03.title: Nevada District 3 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: NV-3 — southern Las Vegas Valley, Henderson and suburban Clark County; a middle-class suburban swing seat. Rated Lean D by Cook, Inside Elections and Sabato (see Race Outlook).
  • Incumbent Status: Susie Lee (D), in Congress since 2019, seeking a fifth term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Lee 69.2%; Republicans — Marty O'Donnell won a crowded primary with 42.3% on June 9. November ballot: Susie Lee (D) and Marty O'Donnell (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Susie Lee (D), an Appropriations Committee member and founder of an after-school nonprofit, faces Marty O'Donnell (R), the video-game composer best known for the Halo series, who lost the 2024 Republican primary here.
  • Voting History: Lee won 51.4% to 48.6% over Drew Johnson in 2024 (+2.8) and 52.0% to 48.0% over April Becker in 2022 (+4.0).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: The drop in Las Vegas visitors, especially from Canada and Mexico, hits suburban hospitality workers; housing affordability, water supply and fuel prices are other top concerns.
  • National Alignment: Lee runs on lowering costs, healthcare and protecting Nevada's tourism economy from trade fallout; O'Donnell runs as a political outsider on taxes, public safety and the Trump agenda.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Lean D (Sept 25); Inside Elections Lean D (Oct 1); Sabato Leans D (Sept 29). Fundraising is competitive — Lee had raised $3.9M in FEC reports as of May 13 and O'Donnell about $4.0M at June 30. No public district poll was found as of 3 October.

NY-03.title: New York District 3 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Affluent North Shore of Long Island — northern Nassau, a slice of western Suffolk and north-eastern Queens. About a quarter of residents are Asian American. Trump carried it 51.4% to 47.1% in 2024, making it a Trump-won seat held by a Democrat. Lines unchanged for 2026: the court-ordered NY-11 redraw was stayed by the U.S. Supreme Court on March 2 and did not affect NY-3.
  • Incumbent Status: Rep. Tom Suozzi (D), back in the House since a February 2024 special election after George Santos's expulsion (he previously held the seat 2017–2023). He is seeking re-election.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Suozzi 79.3%, Danielle Welch 20.5%; Republicans — Mike LiPetri 81.9%, Greg Hach 17.2% in the June 23 primary. November ballot: Tom Suozzi (D) and Mike LiPetri (R, Conservative), per Wikipedia's race page; third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: A rematch: Tom Suozzi (D), a centrist former Nassau County executive, faces Mike LiPetri (R), a former state assemblyman who lost to him by 3.6 points in 2024.
  • Voting History: Suozzi beat LiPetri 51.8% to 48.2% in 2024 (+3.6). In 2022 the seat went to Republican George Santos, who beat Robert Zimmerman 53.8% to 46.2% (+7.6).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Cost of living and property taxes dominate in a district where SALT relief matters. Suozzi has taken criticism from his own base over his shifting stance on Department of Homeland Security funding amid fights over ICE enforcement. Trump, JD Vance and Mike Johnson have all appeared in Nassau to boost Republicans.
  • National Alignment: Suozzi runs on a five-point affordability plan built around "reasonable tariffs, not these reckless tariffs" and calls LiPetri "100% all MAGA". LiPetri defends tariffs as "a tool that's used to rebuild our supply chains" and points to his pro-choice position as a break with Trump. Both have clashed over Israel, Iran and healthcare costs.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Lean D (Sept 25); Inside Elections Lean D (Oct 1); Sabato Leans D (Sept 29). No public polls. Spending is about $19M, including roughly $11M from a pro-Trump super PAC (CBS New York, Oct 2). At June 30, Suozzi had raised $5.46M with $5.68M cash on hand; LiPetri had raised $1.67M with $724K on hand.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Suozzi was named Democratic vice-chair of the Congressional Caucus on India and Indian Americans on March 30, 2026, and is a long-standing member. He has called the US–India relationship "one of the most consequential alliances across the globe today". The district has a significant Indian-American population (Hicksville, Bellerose and north-east Queens). Suozzi also holds a leadership role in the Congressional Pakistan Caucus, giving him an active profile on both India and Pakistan. He voted for H.R. 5334 when the House concurred in the Senate amendments on 16 September 2026 (Roll Call 308, 262–159); the act, enacted on 18 September (Public Law 119-111), authorises duties of up to 100% on countries buying Russian-origin crude oil or gas, which bears directly on India's Russian energy imports. No India-specific position by LiPetri was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

He voted for H.R. 5334 when the House concurred in the Senate amendments on 16 September 2026 (Roll Call 308, 262–159); the act, enacted on 18 September (Public Law 119-111), authorises duties of up to 100% on countries buying Russian-origin crude oil or gas, which bears directly on India's Russian energy imports. No India-specific position by LiPetri was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

NY-04.title: New York District 4 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Central and southern Nassau County on Long Island — Hempstead town communities including Rockville Centre, Long Beach, Valley Stream, Freeport and Garden City. It is the second-wealthiest district in New York. Harris carried it 50.0% to 48.8% in 2024. Lines unchanged for 2026: the court-ordered NY-11 redraw was stayed by the U.S. Supreme Court on March 2 and did not affect NY-4.
  • Incumbent Status: Rep. Laura Gillen (D), in office since January 2025, seeking a second term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Gillen unopposed. Republicans — Jeanine Driscoll 90.8%, Marvin Williams 8.9% in the June 23 primary. Republicans had hoped for a rematch with former Rep. Anthony D'Esposito, but Driscoll became the nominee instead. November ballot: Laura Gillen (D), Jeanine Driscoll (R, Conservative) and Blay Tarnoff (Libertarian), per Wikipedia's race page; not checked against the State Board of Elections certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Laura Gillen (D), an attorney and former Hempstead town supervisor, faces Jeanine Driscoll (R), the Town of Hempstead's receiver of taxes.
  • Voting History: Gillen unseated Anthony D'Esposito 51.1% to 48.9% in 2024 (+2.2), reversing her 2022 loss to him, 48.2% to 51.8% (−3.6).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Property taxes and the cost of living in Nassau lead; Driscoll's platform centres on property-tax relief. Gillen highlights local infrastructure: $125M in federal authorisation for Long Island water projects (Sept 17) and accessibility funding for the Bellerose LIRR station (Sept 8). She is also pushing a bipartisan commuter tax deduction.
  • National Alignment: Gillen campaigns as a bipartisan centrist and co-sponsors bills with Republicans on commuting costs, insurance fraud and newborn screening. Driscoll runs on affordability and taxes. Neither candidate's detailed positions on tariffs, Iran or immigration could be confirmed from sources reviewed.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Lean D (Sept 25); Inside Elections Tilt D (Oct 1); Sabato Leans D (Sept 29). No recent public polls. At June 30, Gillen had raised $5.10M with $3.84M cash on hand, while Driscoll had raised $265K with $226K on hand.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Gillen spoke at a Jan 31, 2026 Indian Republic Day celebration in New York, recalling her work with Mother Teresa in Kolkata and pledging support for the Indian-American community. Asian Americans are about 7% of district residents. No India-specific position by Driscoll was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

NY-17.title: New York District 17 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Lower Hudson Valley suburbs — all of Rockland and Putnam counties plus northern Westchester and part of southern Dutchess. Harris carried it by about half a point in 2024 (50% to 49%), making it one of three Harris-won seats held by a Republican. Lines unchanged for 2026: a state court's January 2026 order to redraw NY-11 was stayed by the U.S. Supreme Court on March 2, and NY-17 was not affected.
  • Incumbent Status: Rep. Mike Lawler (R), in office since January 2023, seeking a third term on the Republican and Conservative lines. He passed up a run for governor to stay in the race.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Cait Conley 49.6%, Beth Davidson 31.8%, Effie Phillips-Staley 15.3% in the June 23 primary (primary field; percentages per Wikipedia's final count). Three other Democrats withdrew before the vote. The Republican primary was cancelled because Lawler was unopposed. November ballot: Cait Conley (D) and Mike Lawler (R, Conservative); the Working Families line could not be confirmed (earlier reports placed Phillips-Staley on it, while the PoliAgg tracker lists Conley), and third-party/independent candidates were not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Mike Lawler (R), a former political consultant and state assemblyman, faces Cait Conley (D), an Army veteran and former National Security Council director for counterterrorism.
  • Voting History: Lawler won 52.1% to 45.8% over Mondaire Jones in 2024 (+6.3), with Anthony Frascone (Working Families) at 2.0%. In 2022 he unseated Sean Patrick Maloney 50.3% to 49.7% (+0.6).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Data centres are a flashpoint. Conley attacks Lawler over five facilities in Rockland and his Big Tech donations, while Lawler says they were built before he entered Congress (News 12 debate, Sept 28). Lawler's push to reopen the Indian Point nuclear plant has drawn opposition from Rockland legislators. Costs and the SALT deduction, which Lawler fought to raise from $10,000 to $40,000, also matter in this high-tax suburb.
  • National Alignment: Lawler runs on the 2025 tax law and the higher SALT cap, says he does not always agree with Trump, and attacks Conley over New York's sanctuary law. Conley says Lawler votes "the Donald Trump way" and attacks him over Medicaid cuts and tariffs. She also highlights his repeated votes to continue the Iran military campaign.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Toss Up (Sept 25); Inside Elections Toss-up (Oct 1); Sabato Toss-up (Sept 29; moved from Lean R on July 30). Emerson/PIX11 (Sept 27–29, 400 LV, ±4.9) has Conley 48%, Lawler 46%. Earlier polls were partisan: a House Majority PAC poll by FM3 had Conley up 51–45 (June 30, per the PoliAgg tracker), and a co/efficient poll for the Lawler campaign had Lawler up 50–45 (July 21, per the PoliAgg tracker). At June 30, Lawler had raised $8.2M with $4.8M cash on hand, against Conley's $4.3M raised and $1.3M on hand.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Lawler is consistently pro-India in public. He welcomed PM Modi's 2023 address to Congress, calling India "an essential partner in the Indo-Pacific region", and at a Jan 31, 2026 Republic Day event in New York he called the US–India partnership "vital for peace and stability around the globe". No India-specific position by Conley was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

NY-19.title: New York District 19 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Large rural and small-town upstate seat stretching from the Catskills and Hudson Valley to the Southern Tier, Ithaca and the Finger Lakes. It covers all or part of Broome, Chenango, Columbia, Cortland, Delaware, Greene, Otsego, Rensselaer, Sullivan, Tompkins and Ulster counties. Harris won it 50.4% to 48.7% in 2024. Lines unchanged for 2026: the court-ordered NY-11 redraw was stayed by the U.S. Supreme Court and did not touch this district.
  • Incumbent Status: Rep. Josh Riley (D), in office since January 2025, seeking a second term on the Democratic and Working Families lines.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — State Sen. Peter Oberacker 77.5%, Alex Portelli 22% (unofficial) in the June 23 primary, after a Trump endorsement. Democrats — Riley was unopposed. November ballot: Josh Riley (D, Working Families) and Peter Oberacker (R, Conservative); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Josh Riley (D), an attorney and former Senate staffer, faces state Sen. Peter Oberacker (R/Conservative), a retired food scientist and manufacturer from Otsego County.
  • Voting History: Riley won 51.1% to 48.8% over Rep. Marc Molinaro in 2024 (+2.3). In 2022, under different lines, Molinaro beat Riley 50.8% to 49.2% (+1.6).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Utility bills are the defining local issue. Both candidates attack NYSEG's rates and billing errors, and Riley co-sponsored a bill to cap NYSEG rate-hike authority while Oberacker proposes a "Ratepayer Bill of Rights". Rural healthcare access, dairy and farm costs, and the cost of grid upgrades for data centres are also live issues.
  • National Alignment: Trump endorsed Oberacker and calls Riley "a radical Left Extremist". Oberacker runs on affordability and lower taxes. Riley voted against the 2025 tax-and-spending law, campaigns on health costs and corporate utility rates, and stresses bipartisan work, including support for Republican-backed border measures.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Likely D (Sept 25); Inside Elections Likely D (Oct 1; moved from Lean D on Sept 17); Sabato Likely D (Sept 29). No public polls. The Congressional Leadership Fund cancelled $4.8M of ad bookings, and the NRCC dropped Oberacker from its programme, after a 2015 Facebook post saluting his grandfather's service in Nazi Germany resurfaced. At June 30, Riley had raised $4.8M with $3.2M cash on hand, against Oberacker's $1.2M raised and $393K on hand.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

OH-09.title: Ohio District 9 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: OH-9 — Toledo and northwest Ohio along the western Lake Erie shore. Ohio's 2025 redistricting redrew the seat to flip it Republican; Trump would have carried the new lines by about 11 points in 2024.
  • Incumbent Status: Marcy Kaptur (D), in Congress since 1983 and the longest-serving woman in House history, seeking re-election despite the hostile map.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Kaptur ran unopposed; Republicans — Derek Merrin won a five-way primary with 44.1% on May 5. November ballot: Marcy Kaptur (D), Derek Merrin (R) and Matthew Althaus (Libertarian), per Wikipedia; not confirmed against the Ohio Secretary of State's certified list as of 3 October; write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Marcy Kaptur (D), a senior Appropriations member known for blue-collar populism, faces Derek Merrin (R), a former state representative (2017–2025) in a rematch of 2024.
  • Voting History: Kaptur edged Merrin 48.3% to 47.6% in 2024 (+0.7) on friendlier lines, after beating J.R. Majewski 56.6% to 43.4% in 2022 (+13.2).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Auto manufacturing — including Toledo's Jeep assembly complex — and steel and glass jobs exposed to tariffs and the Canada trade dispute; Lake Erie water quality and algal blooms are perennial local issues.
  • National Alignment: Kaptur runs as a pro-worker, trade-sceptic Democrat with deep local roots and appropriations clout; Merrin runs on Trump's agenda, taxes and border security in a seat redrawn in his favour.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Toss Up (Sept 25); Inside Elections Tilt R (Oct 1); Sabato Toss-up (Sept 29). A poll by Republican firm McLaughlin & Associates (Apr 18–20) had Merrin 47%, Kaptur 43%. Kaptur leads on money — $4.3M raised by June 30 against Merrin's $1.5M.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Kaptur voted for H.R. 5334 when the House concurred in the Senate amendments on 16 September 2026 (Roll Call 308, 262–159). The act, enacted on 18 September (Public Law 119-111), authorises duties of up to 100% on countries buying Russian-origin crude oil or gas, which bears directly on India's Russian energy imports. Ohio's industrial and farm exports give India further relevance through trade and market access. No India-specific position by Merrin was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

PA-07.title: Pennsylvania District 7 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: The Lehigh Valley in eastern Pennsylvania — all of Lehigh, Northampton and Carbon counties (Allentown, Bethlehem, Easton) plus part of Monroe. A presidential bellwether: Trump won it 51% to 48% in 2024 (+3.2) after Biden carried it in 2020. Voter registration is nearly even between the parties, with a large unaffiliated bloc. Pennsylvania did not redraw for 2026, so lines are unchanged.
  • Incumbent Status: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R), in office since January 2025, seeking a second term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Bob Brooks 41.0%, Ryan Crosswell 21.3%, Lamont McClure 19.9%, Carol Obando-Derstine 17.8% in the May 19 primary. Republicans — Mackenzie renominated. November ballot: Bob Brooks (D) and Ryan Mackenzie (R), per Wikipedia's race page; unaffiliated Frank Golden and independent Ramon Granados have been reported as running, but third-party/independent candidates were not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October. Green Party candidate Andrew Tupone was kept off the ballot; the PA Supreme Court affirmed that ruling on Sept 18.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Ryan Mackenzie (R), a former state representative, faces Bob Brooks (D), a Bethlehem firefighter and president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association. Brooks is endorsed by Gov. Josh Shapiro, Bernie Sanders and the Working Families Party.
  • Voting History: Mackenzie unseated Susan Wild 50.5% to 49.5% in 2024 (+1.0). Wild had held the seat in 2022, 51.0% to 49.0% over Lisa Scheller (+2.0).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Affordability is the dominant theme. Brooks says "the number one issue I hear… is how unaffordable life is", while Mackenzie emphasises housing and energy-cost bills. Spending had reached $9.4M by June 30, ahead of 2024's record pace. The 2024 race cost a district-record $38M.
  • National Alignment: Brooks runs as a labour-backed populist. He backs Medicare for All, paid family leave and public pre-K, and pledges to "take money out of politics". Mackenzie runs on the 2025 tax cuts and cost-of-living relief and is broadly aligned with the Republican leadership and the Trump agenda.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Toss Up (Sept 25); Inside Elections Toss-up (Oct 1); Sabato Lean D (moved from Toss-up on Sept 29). A Franklin & Marshall College poll (released Sept 19, 357 RV) has Brooks 45%, Mackenzie 40%. An earlier Democratic internal poll by GBAO (June 29–July 2) had Brooks up 47–43.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

PA-08.title: Pennsylvania District 8 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: North-eastern Pennsylvania — all of Lackawanna (Scranton), Wayne and Pike counties plus parts of Luzerne (Wilkes-Barre) and Monroe. A historically Democratic, working-class seat that has trended right: Trump won it 53.8% to 45.4% in 2024 (+8.4), and Cook PVI is R+4. Pennsylvania did not redraw for 2026, so lines are unchanged.
  • Incumbent Status: Rep. Rob Bresnahan Jr. (R), in office since January 2025, seeking a second term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti won the May 19 primary. She was endorsed by former Rep. Matt Cartwright and is in the DCCC's Red to Blue programme. Republicans — Bresnahan renominated without opposition. General-election field: Bresnahan vs Cognetti. Final primary percentages were not confirmed for this brief. November ballot: Paige Cognetti (D) and Rob Bresnahan Jr. (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Rob Bresnahan Jr. (R), a construction executive (former CEO of Kuharchik Construction), faces Paige Cognetti (D), a Harvard MBA and former Obama-era Treasury adviser. Cognetti has been Scranton's mayor since 2019, first elected as an independent.
  • Voting History: Bresnahan unseated Matt Cartwright 50.8% to 49.2% in 2024 (+1.6). Cartwright had held it in 2022, 51.2% to 48.8% over Jim Bognet (+2.4).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Ethics dominates. Democrats attack Bresnahan's roughly 650 stock trades since taking office, made despite his pledge to back a congressional trading ban. They include a sale of Medicaid-insurer shares a week before his vote for the 2025 tax-and-spending law with its Medicaid cuts. Republicans counter with a Politico report on a state grant Cognetti secured for a bank where a relative sits on the board. Medicaid and the area's health-care economy are central.
  • National Alignment: Cognetti runs on anti-corruption and cost of living: "We are tired of Washington politicians enriching themselves while selling us out." She is backed by the state AFL-CIO and teachers' union. Bresnahan backed the 2025 tax law and stresses his committee work on transport, small business and agriculture. He has union endorsements of his own (Pennsylvania Teamsters, state troopers, AFGE).

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Toss Up (Sept 25); Inside Elections Toss-up (Oct 1); Sabato Toss-up (Sept 29). No independent polls. Two Democratic-firm polls show Cognetti narrowly ahead: Lake Research Partners (June 22, per the PoliAgg tracker) 47–45 and Impact Research (June 10, 500 LV) 46–45.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

PA-10.title: Pennsylvania District 10 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: South-central Pennsylvania — all of Dauphin County (Harrisburg, the state capital) plus parts of Cumberland and York counties, including the city of York. Trump carried it 52.0% to 46.8% in 2024 (+5.2). Pennsylvania did not redraw its congressional map for 2026, so lines are unchanged.
  • Incumbent Status: Rep. Scott Perry (R), in the House since January 2013 (PA-10 since 2019), seeking an eighth term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Janelle Stelson won the May 19 primary, defeating Dauphin County Commissioner Justin Douglas and others. Republicans — Perry was renominated. Final primary percentages were not confirmed for this brief. November ballot: Janelle Stelson (D), Scott Perry (R) and Isabelle Harman (independent), per Ballotpedia (Aug 3); not checked against the Pennsylvania Department of State certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: A 2024 rematch: Scott Perry (R), a retired Army National Guard brigadier general and former House Freedom Caucus chair, faces Janelle Stelson (D), a former WGAL news anchor of 26 years who left the Republican Party in 2023 over abortion rights.
  • Voting History: Perry beat Stelson 50.6% to 49.4% in 2024 (+1.2). He beat Shamaine Daniels 53.8% to 46.2% in 2022 (+7.6).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Perry's record is the core issue: his role in efforts to overturn Pennsylvania's 2020 result and his hard-right voting record against Stelson's message of accountability and anti-careerism. Costs, congressional stock trading (Stelson backs a ban and 12-year term limits) and abortion access feature heavily in the Harrisburg–York suburbs.
  • National Alignment: Stelson opposes the Trump administration's tariffs and the 2026 Iran war, saying the money should go to the middle class instead. She wants ICE held accountable for deaths in custody and backs government drug-price negotiation. Perry is a hard-line conservative, an ally of Trump who backs tariffs, and a long-standing opponent of large foreign-aid packages.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Toss Up (Sept 25); Inside Elections Toss-up (Oct 1); Sabato Toss-up (Sept 29); see the PoliAgg ratings tracker. A Franklin & Marshall College poll (released Sept 19, 390 RV) has Stelson 47%, Perry 44%. Earlier Public Policy Polling surveys classed as Democratic-aligned by the PoliAgg tracker (July and November 2025) had Stelson up 3–4. At June 30, Stelson had raised $6.36M to Perry's $5.19M.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Perry voted for H.R. 5334 when the House concurred in the Senate amendments on 16 September 2026 (Roll Call 308, 262–159). The act, enacted on 18 September (Public Law 119-111), authorises duties of up to 100% on countries buying Russian-origin crude oil or gas, which bears directly on India's Russian energy imports. Perry's South Asia relevance is security-focused (China, counter-terrorism) rather than diaspora-driven. Senate-AK.title: Alaska (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Alaska — U.S. Senate; a Republican-leaning state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, but with a large independent electorate and a top-four primary with ranked-choice general election that rewards crossover appeal.
  • Incumbent Status: Dan Sullivan (R), two-term senator since 2015, seeking a third term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): In the August 18, 2026 nonpartisan top-four primary (official results, Alaska Division of Elections), Mary Peltola (D) took 49.5%, Dan S. Sullivan (R) 41.4%, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. (R) 2.5%, David Leslie (D) 1.1% and Gerald Heikes (R) 1.05%. November ballot (certified, Division of Elections candidate list): Mary Peltola (D), Dan S. Sullivan (R), Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. (R) and Gerald Heikes (R) — Heikes appears in place of fourth-placed Leslie — plus certified write-ins Sidney Hill (undeclared) and Heather McElwain (Libertarian); the general election uses ranked-choice voting.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Dan Sullivan (R), a Marine Corps Reserve officer and Armed Services Committee member, faces Mary Peltola (D), a Yup'ik former congresswoman (2022–2025) with strong bipartisan appeal and a fisheries-and-families message.
  • Voting History: Sullivan won comfortably in 2020, 53.9% to 41.2% over independent Al Gross (+12.7), after narrowly unseating Democrat Mark Begich in 2014, 48.0% to 45.8% (+2.2).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Affordability is the top concern for 42% of likely voters, led by groceries and fuel; diesel hit $6.66 a gallon in late September amid the Iran war, which Sullivan has backed. Fisheries and energy development remain core Alaskan issues.
  • National Alignment: Peltola runs on cost of living, fisheries and a 'pro-fish, pro-family' independent brand; Sullivan runs on defence, resource development and his alignment with the Trump administration on energy.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook rates the race Toss Up (Sept 23); Inside Elections Lean D and Sabato Toss-up (late September, per Wikipedia's ratings table dated Sept 22–26). An AARP poll (Sept 8–11; bipartisan, by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research; 800 likely voters) has Peltola leading Sullivan 46% to 41% in the first round and winning 53% to 47% after ranked-choice tabulation; she is viewed net-positively (+6) while Sullivan is underwater (–4), especially with independents.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues

Senate-AR.title: Arkansas (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Arkansas — U.S. Senate; a deeply Republican state (Trump +31 in 2024).
  • Incumbent Status: Tom Cotton (R), in office since 2015 and chair of the Senate Republican Conference and the Intelligence Committee, seeking a third term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Cotton 81.6%, Ashby 9.2%, Little 9.1%; Democrats — Shoffner 78.3%, Dunbar 21.7% in the March 3, 2026 primary. sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Tom Cotton (R), an Army veteran of Iraq and Afghanistan and a leading national-security hawk, faces Hallie Shoffner (D), a farmer and entrepreneur endorsed by former Sen. Blanche Lincoln and Gov. Mike Beebe.
  • Voting History: Cotton won 66.5% to 33.5% in 2020 against only a Libertarian, after unseating Democrat Mark Pryor 56.5% to 39.4% in 2014 (+17.1).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Farm-economy stress from tariffs and input costs, rural hospital closures and Medicaid cuts frame Shoffner's challenge in an agricultural state.
  • National Alignment: Cotton runs on national security, China hawkishness and alignment with Trump; Shoffner runs as a pragmatic farmer focused on rural economics and healthcare.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:

Partners (Aug 14–18) had Cotton 51%–35%, while a Hendrix College poll (Aug 11–12) showed Shoffner 47%, Cotton 44%. Cotton held $9.9M cash on hand at June 30 to Shoffner's $863K.

Senate-GA.title: Georgia (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Georgia — U.S. Senate; a Sun Belt swing state Trump carried by 2.2 points in 2024, and one of Republicans' top pickup targets. Rated Likely Democrat (September 2026) by Cook Political Report.
  • Incumbent Status: Jon Ossoff (D), first term; in office since January 2021 and seeking a second term.
  • Top Contenders (certified primary results): Democrats — Ossoff ran unopposed; Republicans — Collins 40.5%, Dooley 30.2%, Carter 25.1% in the May 19 primary, before Collins beat Dooley 55.5% to 44.5% in the June 16 runoff to win the nomination. November ballot: Jon Ossoff (D) and Mike Collins (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Jon Ossoff (D), a former investigative-documentary producer, faces Mike Collins (R), a two-term congressman from GA-10 and trucking-business owner who won the runoff after a last-minute Trump endorsement.
  • Voting History: Ossoff took the seat in the January 2021 runoff 50.6% to 49.4% (+1.2) over David Perdue (R), who had won it in 2014 with 52.9% to 45.2% (+7.7). Every Georgia Senate race since 2020 has been decided by under three points.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Health costs lead: Georgia's average net ACA marketplace premiums more than doubled for 2026 after enhanced subsidies lapsed, and enrolment fell by over 500,000. Ossoff ties this to Collins' vote against extending the subsidies; rural hospital access is a shared theme.
  • National Alignment: Collins runs on cost of living, border security and his private-sector record, casting Ossoff as a career politician; Ossoff attacks Collins on health premiums and ethics, including an ethics probe and his backing of compensation for January 6 rioters.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook rates it Likely D (Sept 23); Inside Elections and Sabato also rate it Likely D (late Sept). A Quantus Insights poll (Sept 14–16) has Ossoff leading 49.0% to 44.9%, with a quarter of independents undecided. Ossoff had raised $98M by June 30 to Collins' $7.4M ($42.6M vs $2.1M cash on hand).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Senate-IA.title: Iowa (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Iowa — U.S. Senate; open seat in a farm state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, now unexpectedly competitive as rising farm and fuel costs bite.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Sen. Joni Ernst (R), two terms since 2015, is not seeking re-election.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Hinson 73.9%, Carlin 26.1%; Democrats — Turek 62.6%, Wahls 37.4% in the June 2 primary. November ballot (Iowa Secretary of State candidate list, updated Aug 19): Ashley Hinson (R), Josh Turek (D), Thomas Laehn (Libertarian); write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Ashley Hinson (R), a three-term congresswoman from IA-2 and former TV news anchor endorsed by Trump, faces Josh Turek (D), a state representative from Council Bluffs and two-time Paralympian in wheelchair basketball.
  • Voting History: Ernst held the seat twice — 51.7% to 45.2% over Theresa Greenfield in 2020 (+6.5) and 52.1% to 43.8% over Bruce Braley in 2014 (+8.3).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Farm pressures lead: fuel and fertiliser costs, lost export markets and beef prices dominate, sharpened by the Iran war and a Tyson beef-plant closure hitting Iowa workers. Hinson has broken with the administration on foreign beef imports and, in late September, called for ending the Iran war.
  • National Alignment: Turek calls tariffs "absolutely chaotic" and blames federal priorities for squeezing families; Hinson stresses domestic production, E15 and biofuels, and trade wins such as China's soybean purchase commitments.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings: Cook Toss Up (Sept 23); Inside Elections Toss-up and Sabato Leans D (late September, per Wikipedia's ratings table). September polls conflict: Marist (Sept 17–20) has Turek up 50% to 42%, while Trafalgar Group (released Sept 18, 1,089 LV) had Hinson 44%, Turek 42%; a Fox News poll released Oct 1 (1,008 LV) had Turek 49%, Hinson 47%. Hinson held a clear fundraising edge in pre-primary FEC reports through May 13 ($8.2M raised and $6.0M on hand, against Turek's $3.5M and $0.7M).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Senate-ID.title: Idaho (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Idaho — U.S. Senate; one of the most Republican states, with a fast-growing Boise metro. Forecasters rate it Solid/Safe R (see Race Outlook).
  • Incumbent Status: Jim Risch (R), in office since 2009 and chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, seeking a fourth term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Risch 67.3% on May 19, 2026; Democrats — David Roth won with 61.9% but withdrew on July 28 so Democrats could consolidate behind independent Todd Achilles. November ballot (per Wikipedia's race page; not checked against the Idaho Secretary of State's certified list): Jim Risch (R), Todd Achilles (independent), Natalie Fleming (independent) and Matt Loesby (Libertarian); write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Jim Risch (R), a former governor, faces independent Todd Achilles, a former Democratic state representative, plus independent Natalie Fleming and Libertarian Matt Loesby.
  • Voting History: Risch won 62.6% to 33.2% over Paulette Jordan in 2020 (+29.4) and 65.3% to 34.7% over Nels Mitchell in 2014 (+30.6).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Rapid growth and housing costs in the Treasure Valley, water rights, public lands and rural healthcare — including hospital and maternity-care closures — shape the race.
  • National Alignment: Risch runs on seniority, national security and conservative values; Achilles runs as an independent problem-solver modelled on Dan Osborn's 2024 Nebraska bid, targeting Republicans weary of partisanship.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid R (Sept 23); Inside Elections Solid R and Sabato Safe R (late September, per Wikipedia's ratings table dated Sept 22–26). The polling average on Wikipedia's race page (updated Sept 18) has Risch up about 10 points (42.5% to 32.4%), though an Advanced Targeting Research poll of registered voters (Sept 13–16; sponsor not stated) showed Achilles ahead 50% to 39%. Risch had raised $4.4M to Achilles's $692K by June 30.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: As Foreign Relations chair, Risch is a key voice on US policy toward India, Pakistan and the Indo-Pacific. He voted for H.R. 5334 in the Senate; the act, enacted on 18 September 2026 (Public Law 119-111), authorises duties of up to 100% on countries buying Russian-origin crude oil or gas, which bears directly on India's Russian energy imports. No India-specific position by Achilles was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Senate-IL.title: Illinois (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Illinois — U.S. Senate; a solidly Democratic state anchored by Chicago and its suburbs. Open seat rated Solid/Safe D by Cook, Inside Elections and Sabato.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Sen. Dick Durbin (D), Senate Democratic Whip and in office since 1997, is retiring after five terms.

November ballot: Juliana Stratton (D) and Don Tracy (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Juliana Stratton (D), Illinois lieutenant governor since 2019 and Gov. Pritzker's chosen candidate, faces Don Tracy (R), former Illinois Republican Party chair and ex-Gaming Board member.
  • Voting History: Durbin won 54.9% to 38.9% over Mark Curran in 2020 (+16.0) and 53.5% to 42.7% over Jim Oberweis in 2014 (+10.8).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Federal immigration enforcement in Chicago dominated the primary, with sharp exchanges over candidates' ties to ICE; state fiscal pressures and public-safety debates also feature.
  • National Alignment: Stratton runs as a progressive opponent of the Trump administration on immigration, healthcare and reproductive rights; Tracy runs on taxes, crime and Illinois' economic decline.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Solid D (Sept 23); Inside Elections Solid D and Sabato Safe D (late September, per Wikipedia's ratings table dated Sept 22–26). Stratton would become one of very few Black women ever elected to the Senate. She had raised $5.9M by June 30 to Tracy's $2.5M.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Indian-American Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, a leading House voice on US–India ties, finished second in the Democratic primary and will leave the House; no India-specific position by either nominee was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:

  • Incumbent Status: Roger Marshall (R), a physician, in office since 2021 and seeking a second term.

sections.html:

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Louisiana — U.S. Senate; a solidly Republican Gulf state. The 2026 race was the first under Louisiana's new closed party primaries. Cook rates it Solid R, Sabato Safe R and Inside Elections Likely R.
  • Incumbent Status: Bill Cassidy (R), in office since 2015, lost renomination after a primary dominated by his 2021 vote to convict Trump at the impeachment trial and his criticism of the president.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Letlow 44.8%, Fleming 28.3%, Cassidy 24.8% on May 16, then Letlow beat Fleming 56.9% to 43.1% in the June 27 runoff; Democrats — Jamie Davis beat Gary Crockett 79.9% to 20.1% in the June 27 runoff. sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:

  • Voting History: Cassidy won 59.3% in the 2020 jungle primary outright and beat Mary Landrieu 55.9% to 44.1% in the 2014 runoff (+11.8).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:

  • National Alignment: Letlow runs as a Trump loyalist on energy, border security and conservative social policy; Davis runs on rural healthcare and economic hardship.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:

Senate-ME.title: Maine (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Maine — U.S. Senate; a Democratic-leaning state Harris carried by about 7 points in 2024. Collins is the only Republican senator from a state Trump never won, making this a top Democratic pickup target.
  • Incumbent Status: Susan Collins (R), five-term senator since 1997 and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, seeking a sixth term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Collins ran unopposed; Democrats — Platner 72.1%, Mills 19.3% (withdrawn), Costello 8.1% in the June 9, 2026 primary. Platner withdrew on July 10 amid a sexual-assault allegation he denies, and a July 25 party convention named Troy Jackson the nominee. November ballot (per Wikipedia's race page; not checked against the Maine Secretary of State's certified list): Susan Collins (R), Troy Jackson (D) and Phillip Rench (independent); write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Susan Collins (R), a long-serving moderate Republican, faces Troy Jackson (D), a logger and former Maine Senate president (2018–2024) running a populist, pro-labour campaign.
  • Voting History: Collins won in 2020, 51.0% to 42.4% over Sara Gideon (+8.6), while Biden carried Maine by 9; in 2014 she won 68.5% to 31.5% (+37.0).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Trade with Canada dominates a border economy: 75% of likely voters are concerned about it and 64% disapprove of Trump's handling of the talks; heating-oil and fuel prices are the other top worry.
  • National Alignment: Jackson runs on paychecks and bills, Social Security, Medicare and abortion rights, casting Collins as out of touch with economic pain; Collins runs on seniority, Appropriations clout for Maine and her independent voting record.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Toss Up (Sept 23); Inside Elections Toss-up and Sabato Lean D (late September, per Wikipedia's ratings table dated Sept 22–26). The University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll (Sept 17–21) has Jackson ahead 51% to 47%, within the margin of error; both candidates are viewed net-negatively. Collins had $11M cash on hand at June 30.

Senate-MI.title: Michigan (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Michigan — U.S. Senate; open seat in a Rust Belt swing state Trump carried by 1.4 points in 2024. Republicans have not won a Michigan Senate race since 1994.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Sen. Gary Peters (D), two terms since 2015, is not seeking re-election.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — El-Sayed 48.5%, Stevens 47.6%, McMorrow 4.0% (McMorrow had suspended her campaign); Republicans — Mike Rogers ran unopposed in the August 4 primary. November ballot: Abdul El-Sayed (D) and Mike Rogers (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Abdul El-Sayed (D), a physician and former Detroit health director running on Medicare for All with UAW backing, faces Mike Rogers (R), a former FBI agent and ex-chair of the House Intelligence Committee who narrowly lost the 2024 Senate race.
  • Voting History: Peters won narrowly in 2020 — 49.9% to 48.2% over John James (+1.7) — after a comfortable 2014 win, 54.6% to 41.3% (+13.3).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Trade anxiety frames the race: Trump's 50% tariffs on Canadian goods and Canada's retaliation weigh on the cross-border auto industry. El-Sayed calls the tariffs "chaotic"; Rogers pledges to work with Trump on fixing those that don't work. Data-centre growth and electricity prices are also live issues.
  • National Alignment: Rogers runs close to Trump, on tax cuts, manufacturing and border enforcement, painting El-Sayed as an extremist; El-Sayed runs on Medicare for All, a wealth tax and abolishing ICE, framing the race around affordability and money in politics.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings split — Cook Toss Up (Sept 23); Inside Elections Lean D and Sabato Lean D (late September, per Wikipedia's ratings table dated Sept 22–26). A Marist poll (Sept 24–27) has El-Sayed leading 51% to 44%, with Trump's approval at 41% in the state; the Senate Leadership Fund has pledged $45M for Rogers.

Senate-MN.title: Minnesota (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Minnesota — U.S. Senate; a Democratic-leaning state (Harris +4 in 2024) with a large rural Republican base. Republicans have not won a Senate race here since 2002. Open seat rated Likely D by Cook, Inside Elections and Sabato.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Sen. Tina Smith (D), in office since 2018, is not seeking re-election.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Flanagan 59.0%, Craig 39.4%; Republicans — Tafoya 52.1%, Schwarze 24.0% in the August 11 primary. November ballot: Peggy Flanagan (DFL) and Michele Tafoya (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Peggy Flanagan (DFL), lieutenant governor since 2019 and a progressive who refused corporate PAC money, faces Michele Tafoya (R), a retired NBC sports broadcaster turned conservative commentator.
  • Voting History: Smith won 48.7% to 43.5% over Jason Lewis in 2020 (+5.2) and 53.0% to 42.4% over Karin Housley in the 2018 special election (+10.6).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Federal immigration enforcement in the Twin Cities, after a fatal ICE shooting in Minneapolis, dominates the campaign; costs of living and healthcare follow.
  • National Alignment: Flanagan calls for dismantling ICE and runs on economic populism and healthcare; Tafoya runs on public safety, border enforcement and cultural issues, positioning herself as a mainstream conservative.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook Likely D (Sept 23); Inside Elections Likely D and Sabato Likely D (late September, per Wikipedia's ratings table dated Sept 22–26). The Race to the WH polling average (through Aug 18) gives Flanagan 46.9% to Tafoya's 41.5%. Flanagan had raised $6.5M through the July 22 pre-primary report and Tafoya $4.7M at June 30, with primary rival Angie Craig now backing Flanagan.

Senate-MS.title: Mississippi (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Mississippi — U.S. Senate; a Republican state with the nation's largest Black population share (about 38%). Democrats have not won a Senate seat here since 1982. Cook rates it Solid R, Sabato Safe R and Inside Elections Likely R.
  • Incumbent Status: Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), appointed in 2018 and elected twice since, seeking a second full term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Hyde-Smith 80.8%, Adlakha 19.2%; Democrats — Colom 72.9%, Williams-Till 18.6%, Littell 8.5% in the March 10 primaries. November ballot: Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), Scott Colom (D), Ty Pinkins (independent); write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), a former state agriculture commissioner and Appropriations member, faces Scott Colom (D), district attorney for Mississippi's 16th Judicial District since 2016; independent Ty Pinkins is also running.
  • Voting History: Hyde-Smith beat Mike Espy 54.1% to 44.1% in 2020 (+10.0) and 53.6% to 46.4% in the 2018 special runoff (+7.2).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Rural hospital closures and the state's refusal to expand Medicaid, poverty and agriculture shape the race; Black turnout is the key variable for any Democratic upset.
  • National Alignment: Hyde-Smith runs on agriculture, conservative values and support for Trump; Colom runs as a law-and-order prosecutor focused on healthcare access and economic opportunity.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:

Senate-MT.title: Montana (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Montana — U.S. Senate; open Republican-held seat in a large, rural state Trump carried by about 20 points in 2024, with a strong independent streak and a tradition of ticket-splitting (Democrat Jon Tester held the other seat until 2025).
  • Incumbent Status: None. Sen. Steve Daines (R), in office since 2015, announced minutes before the 4 March filing deadline that he would not seek a third term, in a coordinated hand-off to Kurt Alme, who filed moments earlier.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Primaries held 2 June 2026. Republicans — Kurt Alme 76.1%, Lee Calhoun 14.1%, Charles WalkingChild 9.7%. Democrats — Alani Bankhead 43.6%, Reilly Neill 33.0%, Michael Black Wolf 13.1%, Christopher Kehoe 6.4%, Michael Hummert 3.9%. Libertarian Kyle Austin also won his primary (53.3%) but was disavowed by the state Libertarian Party. Independent Seth Bodnar qualified separately; Bankhead refused pressure to withdraw by the 10 August deadline. November ballot (Montana Free Press election guide, updated 2 Oct): Kurt Alme (R), Alani Bankhead (D), Seth Bodnar (independent), Kyle Austin (Libertarian), Jami Dee Woodman (no party); not checked against the Secretary of State's certified list; write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: A three-way race: Kurt Alme (R), Trump's twice-appointed US Attorney for Montana and former state budget director, faces independent Seth Bodnar, former Green Beret and University of Montana president (2018–2026) backed by Jon Tester and Max Baucus, and Democrat Alani Bankhead, an Air Force veteran.
  • Voting History: 2020: Daines 55.0% to Steve Bullock (D) 45.0% (+10.0). 2014: Daines 57.8% to Amanda Curtis (D) 40.1% (+17.7).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: The Democratic-independent split is the central dynamic: the state party stood by Bankhead while Tester-wing Democrats and labour groups backed Bodnar (Flathead Beacon). Rural healthcare — Medicaid expansion and critical-access hospitals after H.R. 1 — is a leading issue, alongside housing costs and Sentinel ICBM modernisation jobs at Malmstrom AFB, which Bodnar has pledged to protect.
  • National Alignment: Alme runs as a Trump-endorsed conservative stressing prosecution records, deficit reduction and deregulation for housing; he backs congressional war-powers oversight but executive flexibility. Bodnar opposes "chaotic" tariffs that hurt producers, would restore ACA subsidies and protect Medicaid expansion, insists Congress must authorise war, and pairs strong borders with law-enforcement accountability. Bankhead backs universal TRICARE-style healthcare and immigration reform with due process, and signed a Trump-impeachment pledge (Daily Montanan, 22 Sept).

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings — Cook Solid R (as of Sept 23); Inside Elections Likely R and Sabato Safe R (late September, per Wikipedia's ratings table). The independent Rutgers Eagleton poll for Montana Free Press (27 Aug–7 Sept, 845 RV, ±4.2) has Alme 38%, Bodnar 30%, Bankhead 16%, Austin 5%. FEC reports at June 30: Bodnar raised $3.24M ($978k cash on hand); Alme $1.98M; Bankhead under $60,000.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Senate-NC.title: North Carolina (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: North Carolina — U.S. Senate; open Republican-held seat in a perennial swing state Trump carried by about 3 points in 2024. Democrats have not won a Senate race here since 2008. The 2025 congressional remap does not affect this statewide race.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Sen. Thom Tillis (R), in office since 2015, announced on 29 June 2025 that he would not seek a third term after opposing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and drawing Trump's threat of a primary challenge.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Primaries held 3 March 2026. Democrats — Roy Cooper 92.0%, Justin Dues 2.7%, Marcus Williams 2.5%, Daryl Farrow 1.2%. Republicans — Michael Whatley 64.6%, Don Brown 15.6%, Thomas Johnson 5.7%, Michele Morrow 5.6%, Elizabeth Temple 3.8%, Richard Dansie 2.4%. November ballot (certified, NC State Board of Elections candidate list of Sept 21): Roy Cooper (D), Michael Whatley (R), Shannon W. Bray (Libertarian), Michael Dublin (Green); write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Roy Cooper (D), two-term governor (2017–2025) and former four-term attorney general, faces Trump-endorsed Michael Whatley (R), former Republican National Committee chairman (2024–2025) and former state party chair.
  • Voting History: 2020: Tillis 48.7% to Cal Cunningham (D) 46.9% (+1.8). 2014: Tillis 48.8% to Sen. Kay Hagan (D) 47.3% (+1.5).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Cost of living dominates — 86% of voters rate inflation "very important" in the Elon University Poll (21–31 Aug) — and Cooper runs on a "Make Stuff Cost Less" platform. Hurricane Helene recovery in western North Carolina and FEMA reform remain salient (Ballotpedia), as does Medicaid after H.R. 1, given Cooper signed the state's 2023 Medicaid expansion. Republicans counter on crime and election integrity, with JD Vance rallying for Whatley in Greensboro on 21 Sept (WUNC).
  • National Alignment: Cooper campaigns on reversing tariffs, lowering costs and protecting Medicaid, and casts himself as a pragmatist who worked with a Republican legislature; no specific Iran-war position found. Whatley runs as a Trump loyalist on public safety, border security, election integrity and the Trump tax cuts (no tax on tips, overtime or Social Security). Voters lean against the administration: the same Elon poll found Trump approval at 31/54 and 52% opposed to US military involvement in Iran.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings — Cook Lean D (as of Sept 23), Inside Elections Tilt D (as of Sept 17), Sabato Leans D (as of Sept 22), per Wikipedia's 2026 Senate ratings table. The independent Elon University Poll (21–31 Aug, likely voters, ±5.6) has Cooper 49%, Whatley 38%; High Point University/YouGov (3–12 Aug, 800 RV) Cooper 48%, Whatley 41%; NYT/Siena (15–27 June, 601 LV) Cooper 50%, Whatley 43%. At June 30 Cooper had raised $34.98M with $20.72M cash on hand to Whatley's $11.27M and $3.46M; GOP super PACs (Senate Leadership Fund $22.4M) had poured in money between 1 Aug and 22 Sept.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Senate-NE.title: Nebraska (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Nebraska — U.S. Senate (Class 2 seat); a reliably Republican farm state Trump carried by about 20 points in 2024, though Omaha's 2nd District is competitive and independent Dan Osborn came within 6.7 points of Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024.
  • Incumbent Status: Pete Ricketts (R), former two-term governor, appointed in January 2023 and elected to the remainder of Ben Sasse's term in 2024; seeking his first full term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Primaries held 12 May 2026. Republicans — Ricketts 81.5%, Todd Knobel 8.1%, Debb Axtel Schultz 6.0%, Mac Stevens 2.6%, Eric Mortimore 1.9%. Democrats — Cindy Burbank won 89.5% but filed to withdraw on 17 July to help Osborn; the state Democratic central committee voted on 23 August not to fill the vacancy, leaving no Democrat on the ballot (Nebraska Examiner). Independent Dan Osborn qualified by petition; Legal Marijuana NOW nominee Mike Marvin suspended his campaign and endorsed Osborn. November ballot (per Wikipedia's race page; not checked against the Secretary of State's certified list): Pete Ricketts (R), Dan Osborn (independent), Mike Marvin (Legal Marijuana NOW; campaign suspended), Chuck Conboy (America First), Robin Richards (Working People); no Democratic nominee; write-in candidates not listed.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Ricketts (R) faces Dan Osborn (Independent), a former steamfitter, Navy and National Guard veteran and union leader of the 2021 Kellogg's strike, who refuses to caucus with either party; minor-party candidates remain on the ballot.
  • Voting History: 2024 special: Ricketts 62.6% to Preston Love Jr. (D) 37.4% (+25.2). For comparison, Osborn lost the 2024 regular race for Nebraska's other seat to Deb Fischer 53.2% to 46.5% (+6.7).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: The farm economy is central: both candidates attacked Trump's beef-import tariff waiver amid drought, with Ricketts endorsed by the Nebraska Farm Bureau and Osborn by the Nebraska Farmers Union (Nebraska Examiner, 1 Sept debate). Money and independence are the other axis: Ricketts self-funds and attacks Osborn's out-of-state donors, while Osborn casts the race as "a mechanic against a billionaire". Democratic infighting over leaving the ballot line empty continues, including a lawsuit by a defeated primary candidate.
  • National Alignment: Ricketts backs Trump's tariffs as levelling the field, supports continued pressure on Iran and higher ICE funding, and argues Osborn would vote with Democrats. Osborn criticises "blanket" tariffs and wants Congress to reclaim tariff authority, insists war powers rest with Congress while supporting a deterrent Gulf presence, and backs ICE's public-safety mission but not budget increases, with body cameras and accountability.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings — Cook Likely R (as of Sept 23), Inside Elections Likely R (as of Sept 17), Sabato Likely R (as of Sept 22). Polls are close: SurveyUSA (8–13 Sept, 503 LV) Osborn 46%, Ricketts 42%; Wedgewood (14–16 Sept, 500 LV) Ricketts 52%, Osborn 48%; co/efficient, a Republican firm (released 2 Oct, 1,113 LV), Ricketts 45%, Osborn 40%; a Democratic GBAO poll (3–8 Sept) had Osborn 47%, Ricketts 46% (270toWin poll list). FEC reports at June 30: Ricketts raised $11.2M ($6.9M cash on hand); Osborn $5.8M ($2.4M on hand).
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Ricketts, a Senate Foreign Relations Committee member, co-founded the Senate Quad Caucus with Tammy Duckworth (Sept 2024), co-signed a February 2026 letter with Tim Kaine urging an early Quad summit to deepen "strategic and defense cooperation with India", and condemned the April 2025 Pahalgam attack, saying "the United States stands strong with India against terrorism". No India-specific position by Osborn was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Senate-NH.title: New Hampshire (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: New Hampshire — U.S. Senate; open seat in a small, independent-minded swing state Harris carried by 2.8 points in 2024. Democrats have held both Senate seats since 2017.
  • Incumbent Status: None. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D), in office since 2009, is retiring after three terms.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Pappas 65%, Manzur 33%; Republicans — Sununu 69%, Brown 27% in the September 8, 2026 primary. November ballot: Chris Pappas (D) and John E. Sununu (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:

  • Voting History: Shaheen won comfortably in 2020 — 56.6% to 41.0% over Corky Messner (+15.6) — after a tight 2014 race, 51.5% to 48.2% over Scott Brown (+3.3).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: The Canada trade dispute weighs heavily on a border state: 71% of residents disapprove of Trump's handling of it. Property taxes are also on the ballot, with 55% backing a cap on local school-tax increases.
  • National Alignment: Pappas blames tariffs, lapsed health subsidies and fuel and grocery prices for the cost of living; Sununu runs on the economy and jobs, pitching himself as a reformer with congressional term limits and pay cuts for lawmakers during shutdowns.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:

Senate-OR.title: Oregon (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Oregon — U.S. Senate; a Democratic state driven by Portland and the Willamette Valley, with a conservative rural east and south. Republicans have not won a Senate race here since 2002. Forecasters rate it Solid/Safe D (see Race Outlook).
  • Incumbent Status: Jeff Merkley (D), in office since 2009, seeking a fourth term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Merkley 93.2%; Republicans — Smith 29.5%, Perkins 27.1%, Barker 23.3% in the May 19, 2026 primary. November ballot: Jeff Merkley (D) and David Brock Smith (R); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Jeff Merkley (D), a progressive known for filibuster reform and climate advocacy, faces David Brock Smith (R), a state senator from Oregon's southern coast and businessman.
  • Voting History: Merkley won 56.9% to 39.3% over Jo Rae Perkins in 2020 (+17.6) and 55.7% to 36.9% over Monica Wehby in 2014 (+18.8).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Housing costs and homelessness in Portland, wildfire risk and forest management, and the rural–urban divide shape Oregon politics.
  • National Alignment: Merkley runs as a leading Senate critic of the Trump administration on democracy, climate and healthcare; Smith runs on rural economic concerns, timber and public safety.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:

Senate-SD.title: South Dakota (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: South Dakota — U.S. Senate; a solidly Republican farm state that has elected only Republicans to the Senate since 2008. Forecasters rate the race Solid/Safe R (see Race Outlook).
  • Incumbent Status: Mike Rounds (R), a former two-term governor, in the Senate since 2015 and seeking a third term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Rounds 75.8%, McNeal 24.2% on June 2; Democrats — Julian Beaudion was unopposed but withdrew on August 4, and Democrats did not name a replacement. November ballot: Mike Rounds (R) and Brian Bengs (independent); other third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Mike Rounds (R), an Armed Services and Banking Committee member, faces Brian Bengs (I), a Navy and Air Force veteran and former Northern State University political science professor who was the 2022 Democratic nominee.
  • Voting History: Rounds won 65.7% to 34.3% over Dan Ahlers in 2020 (+31.4) and 50.4% in a three-way 2014 race against Rick Weiland and independent Larry Pressler.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Agricultural prices, tariffs and farm input costs, plus property taxes and Native American community needs on the state's reservations.
  • National Alignment: Rounds runs as a mainstream conservative on defence, agriculture and banking; Bengs runs as an independent on farm economics and anti-establishment frustration.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook

Senate-TX.title: Texas (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Texas — U.S. Senate; a historically safe Republican state that Trump carried by nearly 14 points in 2024 (56.1% to 42.5%), now a competitive race after Ken Paxton's defeat of Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican runoff.
  • Incumbent Status: John Cornyn (R), four-term senator since 2002, lost renomination — the first Texas senator to lose a primary to his own party since 1970.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Talarico 53.0%, Crockett 45.7%, Hassan 1.3%; Republicans — Cornyn 41.9%, Paxton 40.8%, Hunt 13.5% in the March 3, 2026 primary, before Paxton beat Cornyn 63.8% to 36.2% in the May 26 runoff. November ballot: Ken Paxton (R) and James Talarico (D); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Ken Paxton (R), three-term Texas attorney general endorsed by Trump, faces James Talarico (D), an Austin state representative and former teacher.
  • Voting History: Cornyn won his last two races comfortably — 53.6% to 43.8% over MJ Hegar in 2020 (+9.8) and 61.6% to 34.4% over David Alameel in 2014 (+27.2).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Paxton's record — a securities-fraud indictment later resolved, a 2023 impeachment acquittal by the Texas Senate and a high-profile divorce — dominated the primary, with pro-Cornyn groups outspending pro-Paxton forces nearly nine-to-one on ethics attacks.
  • National Alignment: Affordability dominates both campaigns: Paxton pledges to lower costs and take on “Big Food” and “Big Pharma”, while Talarico frames the race as a referendum on corruption and the ultra-wealthy.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Cook rates the race Toss Up (Sept 23); Inside Elections Toss-up and Sabato Leans D (late September, per Wikipedia's ratings table dated Sept 22–26). Recent independent polls show Talarico ahead: Siena College (released Oct 3, 615 LV) 51% to 45%; Fox News (released Oct 1, 881 LV) 51% to 49%; Marist (released Sept 23, 1,139 RV) 50% to 44%; 270toWin's five-poll average on Oct 3 was Talarico 49.6%, Paxton 45.6%. Third-quarter fundraising reports are due on October 15.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026.

Senate-WY.title: Wyoming (Senate)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Wyoming — U.S. Senate; the most Republican state in the country, which has elected only Republicans to the Senate since 1977. Open seat; forecasters rate it Solid/Safe R (see Race Outlook).
  • Incumbent Status: None. Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R), elected in 2020, declined to seek a second term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — Hageman 64.9%, Mead 27.8%, Skovgard 2.7%; Democrats — Byrd 79.3%, Benavidez 20.7% in the August 18 primary. November ballot: Harriet Hageman (R) and James Byrd (D); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:

  • Voting History: Lummis won 73.1% to 26.9% over Merav Ben-David in 2020 (+46); Mike Enzi won 72% in 2014.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Energy — coal, oil, gas and uranium — and federal land management dominate a state where the federal government owns nearly half the land; crypto-friendly regulation, a Lummis priority, also features.
  • National Alignment: Hageman runs as a MAGA conservative on energy dominance, property rights and limiting federal regulation; Byrd runs on public lands access, education and economic diversification.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings: Cook Solid R (Sept 23); Inside Elections Solid R and Sabato Safe R (late September, per Wikipedia's ratings table). Hageman's move to the Senate opens Wyoming's lone House seat. No general-election poll was identified as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: TX-15 — the Rio Grande Valley north and east of McAllen, reshaped in Texas's 2025 mid-decade redistricting; 81% Hispanic and Trump +18 in 2024 on the new lines.
  • Incumbent Status: Monica De La Cruz (R), in Congress since 2023 and the first Republican to hold the seat, seeking a third term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Republicans — De La Cruz renominated unopposed; Democrats — Tejano music star Bobby Pulido won 68.0% over Ada Cuellar, in the March 3, 2026 primary. November ballot: Monica De La Cruz (R) and Bobby Pulido (D); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:

  • Voting History: De La Cruz beat Michelle Vallejo 57.1% to 42.9% in 2024 (+14.2) and 53.3% to 44.8% in 2022 (+8.5), as the Valley swung sharply toward Republicans.

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Healthcare costs are emerging as the defining issue in South Texas, alongside border security, immigration enforcement in mixed-status communities and the redrawn map.
  • National Alignment: De La Cruz runs on border security and Trump's agenda; Pulido runs on affordability and healthcare, seeking to win back Latino voters who drifted Republican in 2024.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook

TX-28.title: Texas District 28 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: TX-28 — Laredo and the border counties south and east of San Antonio; 91% Hispanic and Trump +10 in 2024, a margin Cuellar has repeatedly outrun.
  • Incumbent Status: Henry Cuellar (D), in Congress since 2005 and a senior Appropriations member, seeking re-election after Trump pardoned him on December 3, 2025, in the federal bribery and money-laundering case brought in 2024.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Democrats — Cuellar renominated; Republicans — Webb County Judge Tano Tijerina won the nomination (primaries held March 3, 2026; runoff status not confirmed). Green Party nominee Marlón Durán is also on the ballot. November ballot: Henry Cuellar (D), Tano Tijerina (R) and Marlón Durán (Green); any further independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:

sections.html:

sections.heading: Electoral Context
