VA-02.title: Virginia District 2 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Hampton Roads seat anchored in Virginia Beach, taking in Chesapeake (part), Suffolk, Franklin, Isle of Wight and the Eastern Shore; home to the state's largest concentration of military personnel and a large federal and shipyard workforce. Trump carried it by about 0.2 points in 2024 (49.5% to 49.3%), one of the closest presidential results of any district; Spanberger won it 54% to 46% in the 2025 governor's race. The district is unchanged for 2026: voters approved a Democratic mid-decade redistricting amendment on 21 April 2026 (51.7% Yes), but the Supreme Court of Virginia struck it down on 8 May and the US Supreme Court declined to intervene, so the 2021 court-drawn map remains in force.
  • Incumbent Status: Jen Kiggans (R), a former Navy helicopter pilot and nurse practitioner, in office since January 2023; running for a third term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Primaries were postponed from June to 4 August 2026 because of the redistricting fight. Democrats — Elaine Luria 80.3%, Nila Devanath 16.4%, Bill Fleming 2.0%, Patrick Mosolf 1.3%. Republicans — Kiggans renominated without a contested primary. November ballot (certified, Virginia Department of Elections federal candidate list updated Sept 14): Jen Kiggans (R), Elaine Luria (D), Matt Baker (independent; retired Marine colonel), Geral “Bishop” Staten (independent); write-in candidates not listed (candidate surveys: VPM).

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: A third Kiggans–Luria contest in effect: Luria, a retired Navy commander who held the seat 2019–2023 and lost it to Kiggans in 2022, seeks a comeback against the Republican incumbent.
  • Voting History: 2024: Kiggans 50.7% to Missy Cotter Smasal (D) 46.9% (+3.8). 2022: Kiggans 51.6% to Luria 48.2% (+3.4).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: The district's large federal, military and shipyard workforce makes it sensitive to the 2025 federal shutdown, workforce cuts and defence budgets (Virginia Mercury). Healthcare costs are central: Democrats attack Kiggans's vote for H.R. 1 (Medicaid reductions) and the lapse of enhanced ACA subsidies. Data-centre siting, flood-resilience funding and Port of Virginia cargo volumes also feature in candidate forums.
  • National Alignment: Kiggans backed Trump's February 2026 launch of the Iran war while acknowledging its effect on petrol prices, voted for H.R. 1 and for higher immigration-enforcement funding (Virginia Mercury, 28 Sept). Luria calls the tariffs "cost-spiking", opposes the Iran war as "unnecessary and reckless", pledges to restore ACA subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts, and runs on Trump's "abuses of power".

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings — Cook Toss Up (as of Sept 25), Inside Elections Toss-up (as of Oct 1), Sabato Leans Democratic (as of Sept 29), per 270toWin. No recent independent public poll found; a Tulchin Research poll (9–13 July, 700 LV; Tulchin is a Democratic-aligned firm) showed a 47%–47% tie. FEC pre-primary reports (through 15 July): Kiggans raised $5.95M with $3.39M cash on hand; Luria raised $4.66M with $3.58M on hand.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Kiggans is listed as a member of the House India Caucus on the 118th Congress membership list; no India-specific position by Luria was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026. The district's Asian population is about 5.3% (census-based estimate); no Indian-American-specific figure found.

VA-07.title: Virginia District 7 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Suburban, exurban and rural Northern and Central Virginia: south-eastern Prince William County, Stafford, Spotsylvania, Fredericksburg, Culpeper, Orange, King George, Caroline, Madison and Greene. Harris carried it 50% to 47% in 2024 (Cook PVI D+2); Spanberger won it 58% to 42% in the 2025 governor's race. The district is unchanged for 2026: the voter-approved Democratic redistricting amendment was voided by the Supreme Court of Virginia on 8 May, leaving the 2021 court-drawn map in place.
  • Incumbent Status: Eugene Vindman (D), a retired Army lieutenant colonel, in office since January 2025 (succeeding Abigail Spanberger); running for a second term. He sits on the Armed Services and Agriculture committees.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Primaries were held 4 August 2026. Republicans — Doug Ollivant 56.6%, Phillip Harding 30.6%, Ricky Smithers 12.8%. Democrats — Vindman renominated without a primary. November ballot (certified, Virginia Department of Elections federal candidate list updated Sept 14): Eugene Vindman (D), Doug Ollivant (R), Taner Demirci Lopez (Libertarian), Alaha Ahrar (independent), Joshua Ertle (independent), Randall Terry (independent); write-in candidates not listed (Potomac Local).

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Vindman faces Doug Ollivant (R), a Culpeper-based retired Army lieutenant colonel who served two Iraq tours and was NSC Director for Iraq under Presidents Bush and Obama.
  • Voting History: 2024 (open seat): Vindman 51.2% to Derrick Anderson (R) 48.5% (+2.7). 2022: Abigail Spanberger (D) 52.2% to Yesli Vega (R) 47.6% (+4.6).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Data-centre expansion in Prince William and Culpeper is a live issue: Vindman says operators must "pay their fair share" and stay away from homes and schools, while Ollivant calls them a "military asset" best left to localities (VPM Q&A). Utility bills (Vindman opposes the Dominion–NextEra merger) and the district's heavy federal-worker and military commuter population (Quantico, I-95 corridor) shape the cost-of-living debate. A University of Mary Washington debate on 22 Sept was cancelled after Ollivant withdrew for medical reasons; Vindman had not joined it.
  • National Alignment: Vindman supports ending tariffs, calls the Iran war a "war of choice" that should end immediately, opposes H.R. 1's Medicaid changes, and backs conditions on ICE/CBP funding and opposition to mega-detention centres. Ollivant did not answer VPM's questionnaire but supports Trump's handling of Iran and favours natural gas, "clean coal" and modular nuclear to lower energy costs.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings — Cook Likely D (as of Sept 25), Inside Elections Likely D (as of Oct 1), Sabato Likely D (as of Sept 29), per 270toWin. No independent general-election poll found. FEC pre-primary reports (through 15 July): Vindman raised $12.36M with $6.57M cash on hand; Ollivant raised $251,134 with $65,801 on hand.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026. Vindman is not on the 118th Congress India Caucus list (he took office in 2025); the district's Asian population is about 5.3% (census-based estimate).

WA-03.title: Washington District 3 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: South-west Washington: Clark County (Vancouver, in the Portland metro area) plus Cowlitz, Lewis, Pacific, Wahkiakum and Skamania counties and a sliver of southern Thurston — a mix of fast-growing suburbs and timber and river towns. Trump carried it 50% to 47% in 2024 (Cook PVI R+2). Not redrawn for 2026.
  • Incumbent Status: Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D), an auto-repair shop co-owner and Blue Dog Democrat, in office since January 2023; running for a third term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Top-two primary, 4 August 2026: John Braun (R) 39.7%, Gluesenkamp Perez (D) 36.4%, Brent Hennrich (D) 16.7%; Braun and Gluesenkamp Perez advanced. November ballot: John Braun (R) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D) — under Washington's top-two system no other candidates appear; write-in candidates not listed. The progressive Hennrich drew nearly a third of the Democratic vote over her Israel, energy and SAVE Act votes, though all Democrats combined took about 55% to roughly 43% for Republicans (OPB).

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Gluesenkamp Perez faces Trump-endorsed John Braun (R), Washington state Senate minority leader and owner of Chehalis emergency-vehicle maker Braun Northwest.
  • Voting History: 2024: Gluesenkamp Perez 51.7% to Joe Kent (R) 47.9% (+3.8). 2022: Gluesenkamp Perez 50.1% to Kent 49.3% (+0.8).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: The Interstate Bridge Replacement over the Columbia is a defining issue; Braun backs a new bridge but opposes its light-rail component (Seattle Red, 1 Oct). Housing affordability and homelessness rank high — 91% of likely voters say affordable housing is hard to find (DHM/OPB poll). Rural healthcare access and the district's timber and small-manufacturing base, exposed to tariffs, round out the agenda.
  • National Alignment: Gluesenkamp Perez runs as an independent voice: she opposes the Iran war and has voted five times for war-powers resolutions to end it (statement, 23 July), while backing some GOP measures such as the SAVE Act. Braun, endorsed by Trump on 15 April and championing the Trump tax cuts, supports border security but breaks with Trump on blanket tariffs, favouring only targeted tariffs on China and Russia.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings — Cook Toss Up (as of Sept 25), Inside Elections Toss-up (as of Oct 1), Sabato Leans Democratic (as of Sept 29). The independent DHM Research poll for OPB (17–27 Sept, 543 LV, ±4.2) has Braun 46%, Gluesenkamp Perez 44% (48–47 with leaners); Emerson (8–10 July) had Braun 43%, Gluesenkamp Perez 42%. Gluesenkamp Perez had raised $6.29M to Braun's $2.05M by June 30, but Republican-aligned outside groups had outspent Democratic ones $1.7M to $354,000 by late September.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026. The district's Asian population is about 3.6%.

WA-09.title: Washington District 9 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Central Puget Sound: south and east Seattle, Mercer Island, south Bellevue, Renton, Kent, Auburn, Federal Way and SeaTac — one of the state's most diverse districts, about 23.6% Asian American. Harris carried it 68% to 27% in 2024 (Cook PVI D+22). Not redrawn for 2026.
  • Incumbent Status: Adam Smith (D), in office since 1997, ranking Democrat and former chairman of the House Armed Services Committee; running for re-election.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Top-two primary, 4 August 2026: Smith (D) 47.1%, Doug Basler (R) 21.8%, Kshama Sawant (Independent) 17.3%, Melissa Chaudhry (D) 12.5%; Smith and Basler advanced. November ballot: Adam Smith (D) and Doug Basler (R) — under Washington's top-two system no other candidates appear; write-in candidates not listed. Former Seattle councilmember Sawant ran a left challenge over Smith's defence-industry ties and Israel policy, but finished third (Diya TV; election-night shares were lower for Sawant, whose vote rose in late counting).

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: Smith faces Doug Basler (R), a business owner and repeat challenger whom he beat 71.6% to 28.2% in 2022.
  • Voting History: 2024: Smith 65.4% to fellow Democrat Melissa Chaudhry 32.4% (+33.0). 2022: Smith 71.6% to Basler 28.2% (+43.4).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Housing costs and homeownership top both campaigns' agendas (Kent Reporter, 2 Oct). The district's large immigrant communities make ICE enforcement salient — Chaudhry centred her campaign on her husband's 124-day ICE detention. Smith's Armed Services role and defence-industry links were the focus of the primary challenge from the left.
  • National Alignment: Smith calls the Iran conflict Trump's "catastrophic war of choice" and backed the June war-powers resolution (HASC Democrats, 3 June); he campaigns on rent, grocery and fuel costs and a path to single-payer healthcare. Basler offers an "Opportunity Revolution" platform, says he will work with Trump where aligned, and opposes a federal abortion ban.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings — Cook Solid D (as of Sept 25); not listed as competitive by Inside Elections (as of Oct 1) or Sabato (as of Sept 29), i.e. safe Democratic. No general-election polling found. FEC reports through 15 July: Smith had raised $1.88M; Basler $99,241.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: Smith is listed as a member of the House India Caucus on the 118th Congress membership list, and as senior Democrat on Armed Services is central to US–India defence cooperation legislation (NDAA). Third-placed Kshama Sawant was born in Pune and, on Seattle City Council, sponsored the 2023 caste-discrimination ordinance that divided Indian-American groups. The district is 23.6% Asian American; no Indian-American-specific share found.

WI-03.title: Wisconsin District 3 (House)

sections.heading: Seat Overview
sections.html:
• Constituency Profile: Western and south-western Wisconsin, covering most of the Driftless Area: Eau Claire, La Crosse and Stevens Point plus dairy and grain country across some 19 counties. Trump carried it 53% to 45% in 2024 (Cook PVI R+3). Not redrawn for 2026.
  • Incumbent Status: Derrick Van Orden (R), a retired Navy SEAL, in office since January 2023; running for a third term.
  • Top Contenders (primary results): Primaries held 11 August 2026. Democrats — Rebecca Cooke 60.5%, Emily Berge 39.5% (Berge is a former Eau Claire city council president). Republicans — Van Orden unopposed (99.0%, remainder write-ins). November ballot: Derrick Van Orden (R) and Rebecca Cooke (D); third-party/independent candidates not confirmed against the certified list as of 3 October. Primary results per Wikipedia's tabulation of official results.

sections.heading: Electoral Context
sections.html:
• Candidate Snapshot: A rematch of 2024: Van Orden faces Rebecca Cooke (D), an Eau Claire small-business owner who runs as a moderate, rural-focused Democrat and lost to him by under three points last time.
  • Voting History: 2024: Van Orden 51.3% to Cooke 48.6% (+2.7). 2022 (open seat): Van Orden 51.8% to Brad Pfaff (D) 48.1% (+3.7).

sections.heading: Key Seat Issues
sections.html:
• Local Dynamics: Farm-input costs dominate: diesel and fertiliser prices rose sharply after the Iran war began, while tariffs and retaliation weigh on dairy and soybean exports. Rural healthcare is the other flashpoint — Van Orden touts rural-hospital funding in H.R. 1, while Cooke cites a KFF estimate of $7B in federal Medicaid cuts to Wisconsin over a decade (Wisconsin Examiner, 10 Sept). Debate talks collapsed in late September; the pair are due at a joint forum in Eau Claire on 20 October (WEAU).
  • National Alignment: Van Orden is a close Trump ally: he backs the Iran campaign, voted for H.R. 1 (the "One Big Beautiful Bill"), and has said Democrats "invented" the term affordability. Cooke attacks tariffs and the Iran war as driving up farm and household costs, pledges to protect Medicaid and expand Medicare, and backs price-gouging enforcement and housing tax credits.

sections.heading: Strategic Outlook
sections.html:
• Race Outlook: Ratings — Cook Toss Up (as of Sept 25), Inside Elections Toss-up (as of Oct 1), Sabato Toss-up (as of Sept 29). No independent public poll found; Democratic-sponsored polls show Cooke narrowly ahead — FM3 Research for House Majority PAC (20–25 June) Cooke 50%, Van Orden 46%, with Van Orden's favourability 38/53. FEC pre-primary reports (through 22 July): Van Orden raised $7.53M with $4.68M cash on hand; Cooke raised $8.60M but had $1.83M left after a costly primary.
  • Significance for India-US Interests: No India-specific position was identified in the sources reviewed as of 3 October 2026. The district's Asian population is about 2.3%.
